a3112.speech: “If one of these situations were to occur in a week’s time, we would be much better prepared,” he stressed during an online press conference on Wednesday.

a3112.speaker: The organisers of the symposium
a3112.name: The organisers of the symposium
a3112.speech: Insisted on the exclusively humanitarian nature of the symposium, excluding any discussion of regional conflicts or terrorism.

a3112.speaker: General James B. Hecker, commander of USAFE-AFAFRICA
a3112.name: General James B. Hecker
a3112.title: commander of USAFE-AFAFRICA
a3112.speech: “We are not talking about air superiority or conflict. We are talking about how African nations can help one another.”

a3112.speaker: Lieutenant General Oscar Nyoni, commander of the Zambian Air Force
a3112.name: Lieutenant General Oscar Nyoni
a3112.title: commander of the Zambian Air Force
a3112.speech: “The more of us there are, the better it is for us. In short, it is easier to have more people available to provide support rather than fewer people,” he said, underlining the importance of continental solidarity in the face of disasters.

a3191.speaker: Evariste Ndayishimiye, President of the Republic of Burundi
a3191.name: Evariste Ndayishimiye
a3191.title: President of the Republic of Burundi
a3191.speech: “We planted 4.5 tonnes and we expect a harvest of more than 50 tonnes. We want to call on the population to follow this example because the good Lord has given us arable land so that we may exploit it. We would like to be able to harvest 25 tonnes per hectare, but we have not got there yet. We are continuing to carry out research so as to obtain production that would allow us to export the surplus outside the country.” ; He recalled that all properties belonging to the State must be put to use to help carry out agricultural projects aimed at effectively increasing production.

a3191.speaker: Evariste Ndayishimiye, President of the Republic of Burundi
a3191.name: Evariste Ndayishimiye
a3191.title: President of the Republic of Burundi
a3191.speech: “To get there, the population's contribution is indispensable. State civil servants must learn to divide the day into three parts. They must report for their daily activities as usual in order to work the required 8 hours; take 8 hours to attend to their personal activities and rest during the other 8 hours. But if we never work this way, the country will not develop.”

a3191.speaker: Evariste Ndayishimiye, President of the Republic of Burundi
a3191.name: Evariste Ndayishimiye
a3191.title: President of the Republic of Burundi
a3191.speech: Gave advice to people who invest in agriculture, saying that they must not be discouraged because the beginning is always difficult. He asked them to persevere in order to reach their objective.

a3191.speaker: Evariste Ndayishimiye, President of the Republic of Burundi
a3191.name: Evariste Ndayishimiye
a3191.title: President of the Republic of Burundi
a3191.speech: Reported that he is constantly in contact with seed multipliers in order to look together at how to try to improve the quality of the seed that is distributed and thus achieve satisfactory production.

a3191.speaker: Evariste Ndayishimiye, President of the Republic of Burundi
a3191.name: Evariste Ndayishimiye
a3191.title: President of the Republic of Burundi
a3191.speech: After visiting a 2.51 ha wheat field grown on the same hill, he assured that he expects a very good harvest there too.

a3254.speaker: Ejiro Okotie, gender and social inclusion officer, USAID State2State
a3254.name: Ejiro Okotie
a3254.title: gender and social inclusion officer, USAID State2State
a3254.speech: Said that the rationale behind the physical engagement with stakeholders in Kebbi state is to know how far they have gone in their response, approach, and actions against gender-based violence, which she said is paramount in the collective fight against the scourge of gender-based violence which affects not only women and girls but including boys ; Stressed that the sixteen days of activism against gender-based violence by State2State has been on through all their social media handles raising awareness on the menace and calling for collective action: "We are here in Kebbi state to commemorate the day through physical engagement with our stakeholders to get their response, approach, and actions against gender-based violence, we also need practical solutions not mere words" ; Said that the fight against gender-based violence includes people with disabilities and minor ethnic tribes across the state.

a3254.speaker: Halima Hassan Kamba, Commissioner for Women Affairs, Kebbi State
a3254.name: Halima Hassan Kamba
a3254.title: Commissioner for Women Affairs, Kebbi State
a3254.speech: Said in her opening speech that the fight against gender-based violence is total in Kebbi state with the government providing support to victims and even going as far as creating special courts for trials of perpetrators, who were all brought to book, while the government rehabilitates victims to stem stigmatization: "we thank state2state for the physical engagement you remain our partners in the fight against gender violence, on our part we will ensure inclusiveness and prompt action in reported cases of gender-based violence which even boys can fall victims of sexual or moral violence"

a3567.speaker: Situmbeko Musokotwane, Zambian Minister of Finance and National Planning
a3567.name: Situmbeko Musokotwane
a3567.title: Zambian Minister of Finance and National Planning
a3567.speech: Said the development is a significant step for the country in addressing multiple challenges being faced, and that the signing of the agreement is not only a clear testimony of the result-oriented and methodical approach of the New Dawn administration but is also another demonstration of the strong partnership between the US and Zambia. ; “We are glad that the MCC selected Zambia for the development of a second Compact in December 2021, and since then, Government and MCC have, therefore, been developing the second Compact from 2022. The second Compact will focus on the agriculture sector and aims to support the growth of agriculture production and agro-processing” ; “We also intend to propose for consideration for MCC financing to Agriculture Policy Reform and Institutional Strengthening aimed at increasing private sector trade in domestic and export agricultural markets.” ; “We further intend to include on improvement of access roads and internal road infrastructure in prioritized agriculture corridors [farm blocks], and road maintenance and development of Asset Finance project aimed at increasing access to affordable finance for investment in energy, irrigation, logistics, and processing [EILP] assets for agriculture value chains.”

a3752.speaker: Dr Felix Frimpong, lead Researcher of the Ghana Wheat Initiative
a3752.name: Dr Felix Frimpong
a3752.title: lead Researcher of the Ghana Wheat Initiative
a3752.speech: Explained that the initiative aims to establish domestic wheat production, reduce imports, and create economic opportunities for farmers.

a3752.speaker: Dr Felix Frimpong, lead Researcher of the Ghana Wheat Initiative
a3752.name: Dr Felix Frimpong
a3752.title: lead Researcher of the Ghana Wheat Initiative
a3752.speech: Acknowledged the late Prof. Moses Bradford Mochiah, whose leadership laid the foundation for ongoing agricultural advancements ; expressed his profound gratitude to His Royal Majesty, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II and traditional leaders for their unwavering support and commitment to agricultural transformation.

a3752.speaker: Dr Felix Frimpong, lead Researcher of the Ghana Wheat Initiative
a3752.name: Dr Felix Frimpong
a3752.title: lead Researcher of the Ghana Wheat Initiative
a3752.speech: Urged the Varietal Release Committee to fast-track approvals to accelerate production and ensure that farmers can cultivate without delay, noting that protecting intellectual property rights and securing fair market access remain key to attracting long-term investments.

a3752.speaker: Dr Felix Frimpong, lead Researcher of the Ghana Wheat Initiative
a3752.name: Dr Felix Frimpong
a3752.title: lead Researcher of the Ghana Wheat Initiative
a3752.speech: Disclosed that their global partners, Mahindra and Mahindra and Jain Irrigation, bring cutting-edge mechanisation and irrigation solutions, while the India High Commission and ICAR continue to strengthen Ghana-India agricultural cooperation ; noted that beyond wheat, they recognize the contributions of Dr. Kennedy Agyeman in soybean production and Dr Michael Kwabena Osei, whose tomato project with ICAR is now in its second phase ; stated that Barima Farms' journey in Ghana began with the vision of KC Ezhilarasan, who saw the potential for an integrated agricultural model to transform food security.

a3752.speaker: Dr Felix Frimpong, lead Researcher of the Ghana Wheat Initiative
a3752.name: Dr Felix Frimpong
a3752.title: lead Researcher of the Ghana Wheat Initiative
a3752.speech: Reminded the stakeholders that the initiative is more than a launch and described it as a call to action towards collectively achieving wheat self-sufficiency, empowering farmers and building a stronger agricultural future for Ghana.

a4090.speaker: Fareed Zakaria, columnist (article in the Washington Post)
a4090.name: Fareed Zakaria
a4090.title: columnist (article in the Washington Post)
a4090.speech: Underlines the idea that we are witnessing the formation of a new world order, in which the predictability and multilateralism that marked the second half of the twentieth century are being put to the test.

a4090.speaker: World Bank report “Cabo Verde - Navigating Rough Seas”
a4090.name: World Bank report “Cabo Verde - Navigating Rough Seas”
a4090.speech: Emphasises the need for the country to reinforce its resilience and accelerate its pace of growth, as a response to the increased vulnerability generated by the international context.

a4090.speaker: World Bank
a4090.name: World Bank
a4090.speech: Highlights that Cabo Verde’s institutional stability is one of its greatest assets.

a4090.speaker: World Bank report “Cabo Verde - Navigating Rough Seas”
a4090.name: World Bank report “Cabo Verde - Navigating Rough Seas”
a4090.speech: Warns of the importance of strengthening climate resilience, at a time when environmental and sustainability issues remain a priority for the survival of small island States.

a4122.speaker: Ambassador Ombeni Sefue, Chairman of the Presidential Commission on Tax Reforms (Tanzania)
a4122.name: Ambassador Ombeni Sefue
a4122.title: Chairman of the Presidential Commission on Tax Reforms (Tanzania)
a4122.speech: Told reporters in Dar es Salaam that citizens, businesses, investors and other stakeholders are encouraged to submit their opinions through various channels, including online surveys, emails and text messages: “We would like to inform the public that the commission has begun its work and is now ready to engage with all stakeholders, whether individually or through professional associations, business communities and so forth” ; “The commission will ensure that the final recommendations reflect the experiences and input of everyone contributing to improving the country’s tax” ; “To achieve this, the commission seeks to involve as many citizens as possible to identify challenges and gather practical suggestions that will boost government revenue in a more effective manner” ; “We cannot succeed without the input and engagement of everyone. This is a rare opportunity for every Tanzanian to contribute to a tax system that works for all.”

a4122.speaker: Ambassador Ombeni Sefue, Chairman of the Presidential Commission on Tax Reforms (Tanzania)
a4122.name: Ambassador Ombeni Sefue
a4122.title: Chairman of the Presidential Commission on Tax Reforms (Tanzania)
a4122.speech: Urged universities, research institutions and media outlets to actively participate in the process by organising discussions, facilitating debates and raising public awareness about tax reform.

a4122.speaker: Ambassador Ombeni Sefue, Chairman of the Presidential Commission on Tax Reforms (Tanzania)
a4122.name: Ambassador Ombeni Sefue
a4122.title: Chairman of the Presidential Commission on Tax Reforms (Tanzania)
a4122.speech: Said the reforms are being undertaken in response to longstanding complaints from citizens, businesses and investors regarding various challenges associated with the current tax system, and that challenges such as tax assessment and payment procedures, the multitude of taxes and the complexity of processes have sparked concerns: “Taxes are a vital pillar for the development of any nation. We do not believe there is any citizen who is unaware of the importance of taxes, which ultimately finance the development we aspire to and deserve” ; said the government aims to establish a revenue collection system that is simple, fair and transparent.

a4122.speaker: Ambassador Ombeni Sefue, Chairman of the Presidential Commission on Tax Reforms (Tanzania)
a4122.name: Ambassador Ombeni Sefue
a4122.title: Chairman of the Presidential Commission on Tax Reforms (Tanzania)
a4122.speech: Said that over the past three years Tanzania’s economy has grown by an average of 4.7 per cent but tax revenues have only averaged around 12.1 per cent of GDP: “This is significantly lower than the 15 per cent benchmark needed in sub-Saharan Africa to support sustainable development goals” ; said the government has set an ambitious target to raise the tax-to-GDP ratio to 15 per cent by the 2026/27 fiscal year, a move that would greatly enhance the country’s ability to finance development projects and reduce dependency on loans and foreign aid: “Achieving this target will require expanding the tax base, closing loopholes for tax evasion, improving tax collection efficiency and creating a business-friendly environment that encourages entrepreneurship and investment.”

a4190.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a4190.name: Cyril Ramaphosa
a4190.title: President of South Africa
a4190.speech: “South Africa is a constitutional democracy firmly grounded in the rule of law, justice, and equality,” President Ramaphosa stated in an official declaration shared on the South African presidency's website, as reported by APA.

a4190.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a4190.name: Cyril Ramaphosa
a4190.title: President of South Africa
a4190.speech: Addressing critiques of the new expropriation law, clarified that the law does not constitute a policy of confiscation: “The South African government has not expropriated any land. The newly adopted expropriation law is not a tool for confiscation; rather, it is a legal process established by the Constitution to ensure equitable and just public access to land” ; “Like the United States and other nations, South Africa has always maintained expropriation laws that strike a balance between the need for public land use and the protection of individual rights.”

a4190.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a4190.name: Cyril Ramaphosa
a4190.title: President of South Africa
a4190.speech: expressed his eagerness for dialogue, stating, “We look forward to discussing our land reform policy with the Trump administration. We are confident that through these discussions, we can develop a shared understanding of these issues” ; reminded that “the United States remains a crucial strategic and commercial partner for South Africa,” noting that, “aside from PEPFAR Aid, which accounts for 17% of South Africa's HIV/AIDS program, there is no substantial funding provided by the United States in South Africa.”

a4251.speaker: Velli Nyirongo, economic expert
a4251.name: Velli Nyirongo
a4251.title: economic expert
a4251.speech: “I expect the President to address economic recovery and development. He is likely to provide an update on the [ATM] strategy, which he believes will drive economic growth. He may also discuss progress on implementing the Malawi 2063 development blueprint and outline measures to tackle ongoing economic challenges, including inflation,” he said in an interview.

a4251.speaker: Velli Nyirongo, economic expert
a4251.name: Velli Nyirongo
a4251.title: economic expert
a4251.speech: Anticipates that the President will address the fuel crisis, which he believes will be a key topic ; “Malawians want details on the ‘government-to-government’ fuel purchase deal and the potential outcomes of his visit to the United Arab Emirates” ; “President Chakwera is expected to inspire confidence and hope while acknowledging the challenges the country faces. Most importantly, Malawians want to hear strategies for dealing with the aftermath of USaid's departure.”

a4251.speaker: Gift Trapence, Chairperson, Human Rights Defenders Coalition (HRDC)
a4251.name: Gift Trapence
a4251.title: Chairperson, Human Rights Defenders Coalition (HRDC)
a4251.speech: Emphasising the dire state of the economy, high inflation and persistent fuel shortages, believes the President's Sona must go beyond mere speeches ; “HRDC demands concrete plans with specific timeframes for economic recovery, debt and austerity measures, public service reforms, strategies for domestic health sector funding and measures to protect the poor.”

a4251.speaker: Benedicto Kondowe, Chairperson, National Advocacy Platform
a4251.name: Benedicto Kondowe
a4251.title: Chairperson, National Advocacy Platform
a4251.speech: Outlined “a comprehensive” list of expectations and called for tangible measures to address the economic crisis, including inflation, the weakening Kwacha and the rising cost of living ; “With the exit of USaid, we expect a donor exit strategy, fiscal discipline and public sector reforms. It is also essential that he addresses election preparedness, job creation strategies and improvements in the health sector and social protection programmes.”

a4251.speaker: Nickolas Mwisama, Executive Director, Transparency Initiative
a4251.name: Nickolas Mwisama
a4251.title: Executive Director, Transparency Initiative
a4251.speech: Reminded the President that he was elected with a mandate to primarily tackle economic issues ; “But look at where we are five years down the line. We face an unprecedented inflation rate, with the prices of basic commodities rising daily… So, every Malawian expects the Sona to clearly outline measures to address these issues in the short, medium and long terms. He must demonstrate how he is fixing the system on the ground.”

a4251.speaker: Willy Kambwandira, Executive Director, Centre for Social Accountability and Transparency
a4251.name: Willy Kambwandira
a4251.title: Executive Director, Centre for Social Accountability and Transparency
a4251.speech: Warned against what he called Chakwera's tendency to make promises “without following through” ; “We are not expecting much from his Sona; it will likely be a repetition of previous statements. However, this Sona comes at a crucial time when the country is sliding deeper into a financial crisis… under this watch. As this is his final Sona [in this term], we expect the President to provide a self-evaluation of what he has achieved against his campaign promises.”

a4251.speaker: George Chaponda, Leader of the Opposition in Parliament
a4251.name: George Chaponda
a4251.title: Leader of the Opposition in Parliament
a4251.speech: Said the opposition wants Chakwera to address the suffering of the people and present solutions ; “We intend to ask the President questions afterwards about matters affecting the nation.”

a4251.speaker: Moses Kunkuyu, Malawi government spokesperson
a4251.name: Moses Kunkuyu
a4251.title: Malawi government spokesperson
a4251.speech: Insisted that Chakwera is determined to ensure that Malawians do not suffer due to the suspension of aid; without clearly outlining measures being explored in that regard, said: “We still need aid, yes, but Malawians can be assured that their government will find ways of serving them in the absence of aid.”

a4298.speaker: Alliance of Sahel States (AES) / Mali (complaint filed with the UN Security Council)
a4298.name: Alliance of Sahel States (AES) / Mali (complaint filed with the UN Security Council)
a4298.speech: Filed a case against Ukraine, accused of supporting terrorism in the Sahel, on António Guterres’s desk for examination; in 2022 Mali had filed a first complaint against France, accused of supplying weapons and intelligence to the armed terrorist groups.

a4298.speaker: Leading Ukrainian diplomats
a4298.name: Leading Ukrainian diplomats
a4298.speech: The information that went around the world last July featured leading Ukrainian diplomats stating that they had provided support to the terrorists at Tinzaouatène, in northern Mali.

a4298.speaker: Benjamin Netanyahu, Prime Minister of Israel
a4298.name: Benjamin Netanyahu
a4298.title: Prime Minister of Israel
a4298.speech: Insulted António Guterres, UN Secretary-General, at the United Nations; refused to comply with the United Nations’ injunctions on international humanitarian law and with the strong demand for a cessation of hostilities in the Gaza Strip.

a4298.speaker: President of Malawi (79th session of the UN General Assembly, September 2024)
a4298.name: President of Malawi (79th session of the UN General Assembly
a4298.title: September 2024)
a4298.speech: “Africa’s priority is the reform of the Security Council with the allocation of two permanent member seats for the continent”; he welcomed the support displayed on this subject by the presidents of the United States and China.

a4298.speaker: President of the Transition of Gabon
a4298.name: President of the Transition of Gabon
a4298.speech: “Africa is however awaiting broader support from the other permanent members for this initiative,” while at the same time claiming access to the right of veto for African members, in accordance with the Ezulwini consensus, in order to correct the shortcomings in the functioning of the UN.

a4352.speaker: Technical Unit for Monitoring and Support to Food Security Management (Ct-Sagsa), Ministry of Agriculture (data)
a4352.name: Technical Unit for Monitoring and Support to Food Security Management (Ct-Sagsa)
a4352.title: Ministry of Agriculture (data)
a4352.speech: According to its data, the FAO food price index showed a slight decline for the month of July 2024, and it indicates that the measure temporarily banning the export of food crops in Benin is bearing fruit ; according to its agricultural market data, the fall in cereal prices (-3.8%) offset a rise in the prices of vegetable oils (+2.4%), meat products (+1.2%) and sugar (+0.7%), while the dairy price index remained almost unchanged ; reports that compared with previous years the price levels observed during July 2024 remain high, mainly because of the effects of the Russia-Ukraine crisis ; also notes that the price situation observed in Benin broadly follows the same month-on-month trend as that recorded internationally.

a4352.speaker: Technical Unit for Monitoring and Support to Food Security Management (Ct-Sagsa), Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries
a4352.name: Technical Unit for Monitoring and Support to Food Security Management (Ct-Sagsa)
a4352.title: Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries
a4352.speech: Points out that "Given the high cost of living in this lean season, there is an urgent need to strengthen support measures for the population, particularly the most vulnerable groups" ; recommends among the actions to be taken: strengthening the monitoring of the implementation of the temporary ban on the export of food crops from the national territory; accelerating the implementation of the Special Program for the Intensification of Vegetable and Cereal Production; setting up a system for collecting statistics on flows at the major collection sites and at the borders, as well as setting up a system for monitoring and reporting information on disasters recorded in the communes that could compromise the results of the season.

a4369.speaker: Christian Sedat, German Ambassador to South Sudan
a4369.name: Christian Sedat
a4369.title: German Ambassador to South Sudan
a4369.speech: Said his government is happy to support the first independent radio station in the country in its determination to extend coverage to Yambio and Aweil, and said in an interview with Eye Radio that the intervention came after the management of Eye Radio reached out to the Embassy requesting technical support to fix the power issues that affected the Yambio and Aweil repeaters ; “Eye Radio reached out to Germany Embassy several months ago and pointed to several technical difficulties in the transmission throughout the country and we have looked into it and we provided support for two regions of Aweil and Yambio.” ; “Then what is celebratory to announce is that due to this support of the Germany Embassy, listeners in Yambio are back on air. So, I want to say special greetings to your listeners in Yambio and welcome back.”

a4369.speaker: Stephen Omiri, Chief Executive Officer of Eye Media
a4369.name: Stephen Omiri
a4369.title: Chief Executive Officer of Eye Media
a4369.speech: Said the relay station in Yambio went off air after the state’s electricity company introduced a cost reduction in its power supply approximately in July 2024; welcoming Germany’s support, said the solar power system in Yambio and a similar installation to be made in Aweil in Northern Bahr el Ghazal will keep the repeaters operating without power interruptions; and said the station intends to install similar power systems in Bor, Malakal, Baliet, and Kuajok with funding from the U.S. government through USAID ; “Our transmitter requires a lot of power so we went off air and we have to now go around and look for funding from well wishers and we wrote a couple of letters good enough we were lucky to get reply from Germany Embassy.” ; “The German Embassy were able to give us $24,995 to restore back the power, buy batteries and solar panels to ensure that Yambio and Aweil are back on air. So, we are really grateful to the embassy because you see it is going to allow people of Yambio to have access to information.”

a4369.speaker: Emmanuel Kenyi, Eye Media technician
a4369.name: Emmanuel Kenyi
a4369.title: Eye Media technician
a4369.speech: Assured the people of Yambio that the new solar power system installed there has a capability of about 15 years: “I will anticipate that even without sunshine, we will still go for more than 17 hours [because] the battery bank is huge, I will say that Yambio will always be on because the power is massive and technically solar panels last for 30 years. So the system we have installed in Yambio can stay for more than 15 years.”

a4428.speaker: Sir Comércio Internacional (company declaration)
a4428.name: Sir Comércio Internacional (company declaration)
a4428.speech: In 2023, as part of a broader protest by several Mozambican organizations against Israel’s occupation of Palestine, joined the initiative by declaring its refusal to sell Israeli products, aligning itself with the unofficial “Israeli apartheid-free zone.”

a4516.speaker: Ministry (of Defence, Namibia)
a4516.name: Ministry (of Defence
a4516.title: Namibia)
a4516.speech: "Although the fairs are mainly geared towards learners, we warmly welcome community members to stop by our exhibition stand. It is a great chance to explore exciting career opportunities in the Namibian Defence Force and learn more about the important work our soldiers do," the ministry said yesterday.

a4653.speaker: AFRICOM (US Africa Command)
a4653.name: AFRICOM (US Africa Command)
a4653.speech: said on Saturday that the U.S. military carried out an airstrike targeting Islamic State militants southeast of Bosaso on Friday, in coordination with Somalia’s federal government, amid ongoing counterinsurgency operations in the region.

a4903.speaker: Trump administration
a4903.name: Trump administration
a4903.speech: Said Lesotho, a small landlocked kingdom, is hit with the highest tariff, 50%, because of its own tariffs of 99% on American products.

a4903.speaker: Meissa Babou, Senegalese economist
a4903.name: Meissa Babou
a4903.title: Senegalese economist
a4903.speech: “These measures mark a significant break with the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), a long-standing trade agreement aimed at supporting African development by offering preferential access to American markets. And so, it will be dramatic for the products or exporters that had specialised in this American market,” analyses the Senegalese economist Meissa Babou.

a4903.speaker: Meissa Babou, Senegalese economist
a4903.name: Meissa Babou
a4903.title: Senegalese economist
a4903.speech: Said African countries do not have the capacity to respond to this American provocation because they already import everything. “If we follow this logic, we will create domestic inflation at home, because the 10% increase in duties risks creating a surge in prices here. And so, I believe it is not very intelligent to want to follow Donald Trump in this logic of a trade war” ; since the importer position does not allow guaranteeing sufficient local production, “we must remain calm and not respond to this American commercial aggression.”

a4903.speaker: Meissa Babou, Senegalese economist
a4903.name: Meissa Babou
a4903.title: Senegalese economist
a4903.speech: Believes the Asian market could be a good alternative: “There could be ways to bypass the American market, provided that exports, even if they are considerable, can be redirected towards other economic zones, such as Asia or Europe” ; but warns that “the advantages Africans enjoyed thanks to AGOA are not found in Europe”. “Indeed, European trade standards, often very demanding in terms of product quality, represent a major obstacle. This complicates access to this market, which is already notoriously difficult to penetrate. Nevertheless, other countries, such as China, offer opportunities. With a powerful economy and an immense population that consumes almost everything, China could represent a promising new avenue for African exporters,” he concludes.

a4903.speaker: White House (data)
a4903.name: White House (data)
a4903.speech: Cited as the source of the table listing the customs tariffs applied by the United States and African countries.

a4951.speaker: Prof. Muhammad Pate, Nigeria's Minister of Health and Coordinating Minister of Health Sector
a4951.name: Prof. Muhammad Pate
a4951.title: Nigeria's Minister of Health and Coordinating Minister of Health Sector
a4951.speech: Says that the Nigerian health sector reforms received global recognition at a high-level event during the 2025 World Bank and IMF Annual Meetings in Washington D.C., themed "Scaling Health Reforms."

a4951.speaker: Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare (statement released through its official X handle, @Fmohnigerian)
a4951.name: Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare (statement released through its official X handle
a4951.title: @Fmohnigerian)
a4951.speech: Said Nigeria's presence and role at the event joined global health leaders, including the WHO Director-General, World Bank President and various Health Ministers, alongside heads of leading pharmaceutical companies.

a4951.speaker: Prof. Muhammad Pate, Nigeria's Minister of Health
a4951.name: Prof. Muhammad Pate
a4951.title: Nigeria's Minister of Health
a4951.speech: Emphasised progress through Nigeria's Sector-Wide Approach (SWAp), aligning government and donor investments with national priorities: "In just six months of 2025, revitalised primary healthcare facilities recorded more than 80 million visits through SWAp, a fourfold increase from the same period in 2023." ; "Through local manufacturing partnerships, we're creating jobs, adding economic value, and building a sustainable base for health delivery." ; added that by 2030 Nigeria aims to produce a significant share of essential health commodities domestically, reducing import dependence and strengthening the resilience of its national health supply chain.

a4951.speaker: Prof. Muhammad Pate, Nigeria's Minister of Health
a4951.name: Prof. Muhammad Pate
a4951.title: Nigeria's Minister of Health
a4951.speech: Noted that Nigeria's multi-donor trust fund and improved partnerships were aligning global funding with national objectives, an approach now showing real impact: "For the first time, development assistance aligns with Nigeria's own goals, not the other way around. That's how reforms move from boardrooms to real impact for people." ; said these health sector efforts are rooted in President Bola Tinubu's Renewed Hope Agenda; noted that Nigeria's participation in the high-level dialogue affirms its growing credibility and leadership in shaping future health systems and reform priorities across Africa and other low- and middle-income countries.

a4951.speaker: Dr Tedros Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General (as reported by Pate)
a4951.name: Dr Tedros Ghebreyesus
a4951.title: WHO Director-General (as reported by Pate)
a4951.speech: Hailed Nigeria's leadership and reaffirmed the organization's commitment to support the country's health transformation, in partnership with Gavi, the World Bank and other actors.

a5028.speaker: Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria (PSN)
a5028.name: Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria (PSN)
a5028.speech: Has lamented the tragic consequences of counterfeit drugs, saying it is a direct threat to the lives of millions of Nigerians, including therapeutic failures, fatalities, thereby undermining the credibility of the country’s healthcare system ; PSN reported that the prevalence of fake drugs has escalated to alarming levels, with over 50 percent of medicines in circulation being counterfeit or substandard, calling for harsher penalties against drug counterfeiters.

a5028.speaker: Pharm Tanko Ibrahim Ayuba, PSN President
a5028.name: Pharm Tanko Ibrahim Ayuba
a5028.title: PSN President
a5028.speech: “Our research shows that the prevalence of fake drugs has escalated to alarming levels, with over 50 percent of medications in circulation being counterfeit or substandard. This is a direct threat to the lives of millions of Nigerians and undermines the credibility of our healthcare system” ; “The unchecked sale of counterfeit drugs in open drug markets has resulted in severe health crises, including kidney and liver damage. These fake and substandard products, often sold at suspiciously low prices, pose life-threatening risks to consumers.”

a5028.speaker: Pharm Tanko Ibrahim Ayuba, PSN President
a5028.name: Pharm Tanko Ibrahim Ayuba
a5028.title: PSN President
a5028.speech: Called on the National Assembly to revisit and strengthen the provisions of the Fake Drug Act, advocating for more severe penalties to deter offenders: “Drug counterfeiting is not just a crime against individuals; it is a crime against humanity. We need legislation that reflects the gravity of this offense, with stricter enforcement mechanisms to protect our citizens” ; “Increasing penalties for drug fakers, coupled with the establishment of well-regulated Coordinated Wholesale Centres, will significantly curb the proliferation of fake drugs and ensure better access to safe and effective medications” ; “Stronger penalties, effective enforcement, and continuous public awareness are the keys to achieving a safer pharmaceutical landscape in Nigeria” ; “We are working tirelessly to engage the highest authorities and have received assurances that these issues will be addressed. However, it is critical to sustain momentum and ensure that offenders face penalties commensurate with the harm they cause.”

a5028.speaker: Pharm Tanko Ibrahim Ayuba, PSN President
a5028.name: Pharm Tanko Ibrahim Ayuba
a5028.title: PSN President
a5028.speech: Lauded recent efforts by the Pharmacy Council of Nigeria (PCN) and NAFDAC, such as the closure of unregulated drug markets like Sabogeri and Onitsha Bridge Market, and stressed the importance of sustaining these collaborations to address the over five million unregistered drug outlets across Nigeria, and that such actions must be consistent and backed by stronger legal frameworks.

a5028.speaker: Pharm Tanko Ibrahim Ayuba, PSN President
a5028.name: Pharm Tanko Ibrahim Ayuba
a5028.title: PSN President
a5028.speech: Emphasised the importance of collaboration among healthcare professionals, government agencies, and stakeholders in combating the challenges of fake drugs and unregulated markets: “Healthcare is a teamwork effort, and pharmacists play an indispensable role in ensuring the safety and efficacy of medications. Unfortunately, some professionals in the health sector assume superiority, disrupting the concept of teamwork.”

a5028.speaker: Pharm Tanko Ibrahim Ayuba, PSN President
a5028.name: Pharm Tanko Ibrahim Ayuba
a5028.title: PSN President
a5028.speech: On patient medicine shops, highlighted their intended role in rural areas and the need for stricter monitoring to prevent abuse: “Patient medicine shops should serve as a last resort where no pharmacies exist. They must adhere to regulations, stocking only approved drugs and selling them in their original containers.”

a5028.speaker: Pharm Tanko Ibrahim Ayuba, PSN President
a5028.name: Pharm Tanko Ibrahim Ayuba
a5028.title: PSN President
a5028.speech: On the departure of pharmaceutical giants like GSK and Sanofi from Nigeria, acknowledged the economic pressures driving such exits, noting that scarcity of genuine products often fuels the market for counterfeits ; appealed to consumers to prioritise safety over cost, encouraging them to purchase medications from licensed pharmacies: “Drugs are not commodities like sugar or tomatoes. They are inherently potent substances, and only pharmacists are trained, licensed, and equipped to handle them safely.”

a5028.speaker: Pharm. Ambrose Eze, National Chairman, Association of Community Pharmacists of Nigeria (ACPN)
a5028.name: Pharm. Ambrose Eze
a5028.title: National Chairman, Association of Community Pharmacists of Nigeria (ACPN)
a5028.speech: Has said that the recent Executive Order by President Donald Trump to freeze the funding of PEPFAR under USAID in January is a wake-up call for Nigeria ; “HIV medication is quite expensive. Despite the funding from the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), some people still do not have access to the drugs” ; “Lack of access to HIV drugs would lead to a spike in the infection, thereby increasing the HIV prevalence rates. Lack of access and lack of availability will make HIV drugs very expensive and unaffordable” ; “Therefore, the recent fund withdrawal directive by US President Donald Trump is a strong signal of the need for African countries like Nigeria to begin to look inward and take over the funding of essential healthcare services from donors” ; “The government should take over the funding of essential healthcare services being driven by donors. So, also public-spirited individuals, private-sector organisations, and bodies in Nigeria should support the government’s efforts.”

a5119.speaker: United Kingdom (announcement)
a5119.name: United Kingdom (announcement)
a5119.speech: Has announced that it will host the 17th Replenishment pledging session of the African Development Fund (ADF) in December, bringing together development partners to agree on contributions for the ADF's 2026-2028 cycle.

a5119.speaker: Baroness Jenny Chapman, UK Minister of State for Development and Africa
a5119.name: Baroness Jenny Chapman
a5119.title: UK Minister of State for Development and Africa
a5119.speech: Said the UK intends to make a strong pledge and encouraged all development partners to consider ambitious contributions to the 17th replenishment of the Fund ; "The replenishment is an opportunity to signal our collective commitment to Africa's growth and development, its institutions, and to innovative, modern approaches to development finance in a challenging global environment" ; noted that the UK remains a key contributor to the Fund, providing substantial financial commitments and strategic engagement that help sustain development impact, even amid a tighter aid budget ; also welcomed Dr. Ould Tah's proposal for the UK to host a Private Sector Day for private companies and development finance institutions.

a5119.speaker: Dr Sidi Ould Tah, African Development Bank Group President
a5119.name: Dr Sidi Ould Tah
a5119.title: African Development Bank Group President
a5119.speech: "The African Development Bank Group welcomes United Kingdom's announcement to host the African Development Fund's 17th replenishment pledging session." ; "It is a rallying call for a strong ADF-17 replenishment, which is both an investment in Africa's development as well as in shared global prosperity."

a5119.speaker: Report distributed by APO Group on behalf of African Development Bank Group (AfDB)
a5119.name: Report distributed by APO Group on behalf of African Development Bank Group (AfDB)
a5119.speech: According to the report, over the past decade the African Development Fund has connected more than 18 million people to electricity and enhanced agricultural productivity for 11 million farmers; it has improved access to water and sanitation for 48 million people and to transport for more than 87 million.

a5119.speaker: Centre for Global Development
a5119.name: Centre for Global Development
a5119.speech: In 2021 recognised the quality of the Fund's development assistance, ranking it second among 49 bilateral and multilateral development agencies.

a5198.speaker: Aaron Sunday, leader of the Association of Positive Youths with HIV in Nigeria (APYIN)
a5198.name: Aaron Sunday
a5198.title: leader of the Association of Positive Youths with HIV in Nigeria (APYIN)
a5198.speech: “The age of sexual debut in Nigeria is often below 18, so policies must recognise this reality to ensure effective HIV prevention and control” ; “We had begun building momentum, holding meetings with local authorities, parents, and health commissioners across states. Then, suddenly, everything stopped.”

a5198.speaker: Officials of civil society organisations and leaders of CSO networks across different states
a5198.name: Officials of civil society organisations and leaders of CSO networks across different states
a5198.speech: Confirmed to PREMIUM TIMES receiving emails suspending ongoing projects with the agency.

a5198.speaker: Abdullahi Ibrahim, Chairman of the Network of People Living with HIV/AIDS in Nigeria (NEPWHAN) Bauchi chapter
a5198.name: Abdullahi Ibrahim
a5198.title: Chairman of the Network of People Living with HIV/AIDS in Nigeria (NEPWHAN) Bauchi chapter
a5198.speech: Described the situation as a serious threat to HIV control efforts in Nigeria.

a5198.speaker: Chris Damcher, chairman of the Plateau CSO Networks
a5198.name: Chris Damcher
a5198.title: chairman of the Plateau CSO Networks
a5198.speech: Told PREMIUM TIMES that most of the intervention programmes suspended in the states focused on addressing health issues ; “The impact has been mostly on healthcare. It affected other sectors directly and indirectly, but the agency contributes significantly to healthcare.”

a5198.speaker: Health professionals
a5198.name: Health professionals
a5198.speech: Have told PREMIUM TIMES that Nigeria is unlikely to receive vaccine donations this year without USAID.

a5198.speaker: CSO Network in Plateau State
a5198.name: CSO Network in Plateau State
a5198.speech: Said some organisations in the state have fully shut down their activities, and those still functioning might be forced to do the same if the order persists after 90 days.

a5198.speaker: Report by the Council on Foreign Relations
a5198.name: Report by the Council on Foreign Relations
a5198.speech: Said no money has been disbursed due to a lack of clarity on interpreting the waivers, and the freeze has continued to cause mass layoffs and suspensions.

a5198.speaker: Musa Umar, lead CSO for the Zamfara Network of CSOs
a5198.name: Musa Umar
a5198.title: lead CSO for the Zamfara Network of CSOs
a5198.speech: Told our reporter that the local staff assigned to execute the project in different communities were called back in January ; “In a case where there are normally five or six non-profits providing different forms of humanitarian assistance to displaced persons, you can only find one or two.”

a5198.speaker: Health advocates
a5198.name: Health advocates
a5198.speech: Said the suspension of these programmes means the support and guidance provided to parents and caregivers under the initiative are currently unavailable.

a5198.speaker: United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF)
a5198.name: United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF)
a5198.speech: According to UNICEF, about 250,000 children are suffering from severe acute malnutrition in Zamfara.

a5198.speaker: Ajah Oliver, executive director of Cooperation Social Responsibility, a non-profit in Ebonyi
a5198.name: Ajah Oliver
a5198.title: executive director of Cooperation Social Responsibility, a non-profit in Ebonyi
a5198.speech: Disclosed that the state relied heavily on USAID funding and that, as a result, the policy ended interventions statewide ; said the agency was also primarily involved in revitalising PHCs in Ebonyi through a statewide Integrated Health programme whose major goal was to improve maternal health by ensuring better access to quality care.

a5198.speaker: Tayo Fatinikun, Executive Director of Life Helper Initiatives, a non-profit in Sokoto
a5198.name: Tayo Fatinikun
a5198.title: Executive Director of Life Helper Initiatives, a non-profit in Sokoto
a5198.speech: Said the US policy should be a wake-up call to the government to strengthen domestic funding for key sectors ; “We can't be dependent forever. The government, both at the state and federal level, needs to step up.”

a5198.speaker: CSO Networks across states
a5198.name: CSO Networks across states
a5198.speech: Told PREMIUM TIMES that the country's health system will likely experience serious setbacks without US foreign aid, and many expressed concern that the likely implication of suspending health interventions would be an increase in the country's disease transmission risk.

a5198.speaker: Chris Damcher, chairperson of the Plateau CSO network
a5198.name: Chris Damcher
a5198.title: chairperson of the Plateau CSO network
a5198.speech: Said the CSOs are engaging with the state government to consolidate the progress made by previous interventions.

a5198.speaker: Larry Garber, adjunct professor at George Washington University
a5198.name: Larry Garber
a5198.title: adjunct professor at George Washington University
a5198.speech: Said the policy on USAID mirrors proposals outlined in the Project 2025 presidential transition plan, a 900-page document considered a policy wish list for the US president.

a5198.speaker: Data from the US Department of State website
a5198.name: Data from the US Department of State website
a5198.speech: According to the data, USAID has provided Nigeria with $6.39 billion in foreign aid in the last decade.

a5232.speaker: Al Jazeera
a5232.name: Al Jazeera
a5232.speech: reported on Wednesday, February 12, 2025, that the rebels had on Tuesday attacked and captured the village of Ihusi, about 40 kilometres from Kavumu airport, which is 70 kilometres from Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu province.

a5232.speaker: Malcolm Webb, Al Jazeera reporter (reporting from Nairobi, Kenya)
a5232.name: Malcolm Webb
a5232.title: Al Jazeera reporter (reporting from Nairobi, Kenya)
a5232.speech: said residents of Bukavu are waiting to see whether M23 fighters will manage to overcome the DRC armed forces (FARDC) and capture the city ; "Some of them are seen packing their belongings to leave in search of calmer areas. Others say they will stay there until things become clear, or until they are forced to abandon their homes because of the war."

a5232.speaker: M23 (public statement)
a5232.name: M23 (public statement)
a5232.speech: issued a public statement on Monday denying that it had driven out civilians who had fled to displacement camps, saying people were leaving the Bulengo camp voluntarily and returning to what it claimed were their homes after peace had been restored by the rebels.

a5232.speaker: 24 leaders of the East African Community (EAC) and the Southern African Development Community (SADC)
a5232.name: 24 leaders of the East African Community (EAC) and the Southern African Development Community (SADC)
a5232.speech: met in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania on Saturday and resolved to require the defence chiefs of each member state to meet and come up with a strategy to end the conflict, having met urgently out of fear that the fighting could turn into a regional war.

a5232.speaker: United Nations
a5232.name: United Nations
a5232.speech: According to the United Nations, the violence has displaced more than 6.7 million people inside the country, many fleeing North Kivu province for South Kivu to escape the fighting.

a5232.speaker: Bruno Lemarquis, senior UN official in the DRC
a5232.name: Bruno Lemarquis
a5232.title: senior UN official in the DRC
a5232.speech: said the fighting has affected the delivery of humanitarian services to victims of the war, and said President Donald Trump's decision to suspend aid through the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) had also had an impact ; "The suspension of funding activities means the halting of emergency programmes, including shelter and accommodation that were being provided to displaced people who are victims of the ongoing war in the DRC."

a5232.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5232.name: Donald Trump
a5232.title: US President
a5232.speech: ordered the suspension of aid and funding by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) for 90 days to allow a thorough review of the agency's performance, a decision he announced hours after being sworn in and taking up his duties as President.

a5232.speaker: Government of President Felix Tshisekedi (DRC)
a5232.name: Government of President Felix Tshisekedi (DRC)
a5232.speech: continues to accuse Rwanda of funding the M23 rebels, whose fighting against FARDC has caused the deaths of more than 3,000 people, and of backing the rebels in order to obtain resources including minerals.

a5232.speaker: James Ng'anzi (Ngango), Rwanda's Ambassador to the UN
a5232.name: James Ng'anzi (Ngango)
a5232.title: Rwanda's Ambassador to the UN
a5232.speech: reiterated President Paul Kagame's denial that Rwanda is involved: "We strongly object to the DRC government's attempt to smear us as being involved in funding the unrest in eastern DRC. We are not involved in that" ; "This matter is clear. But because of the threat of the rebels being in the DRC, the only one to be blamed is Rwanda. After the city of Goma fell into the hands of the rebels, successive attacks have also begun to target Rwanda", while accusing the DRC of scattering weapons around Goma airport, speaking at the emergency session of the UN Human Rights Council.

a5232.speaker: Jean Vianney, leader of the villages attacked (Ituri)
a5232.name: Jean Vianney
a5232.title: leader of the villages attacked (Ituri)
a5232.speech: said the Codeco group's attacks on civilians began on Monday at 8 a.m., in which many people were killed by gunfire, hacked with machetes and burned inside their homes.

a5232.speaker: United Nations
a5232.name: United Nations
a5232.speech: has been accusing Codeco of carrying out attacks on communities, particularly on the Hema ethnic community, and of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity.

a5239.speaker: Professor Ntoi Rapapa, Education Minister of Lesotho
a5239.name: Professor Ntoi Rapapa
a5239.title: Education Minister of Lesotho
a5239.speech: hailed the contribution: "This support comes at a critical moment for these learners and their families, bringing hope to vulnerable children. It demonstrates that united, we can face any challenge. We deeply appreciate ETL, Higherlife Foundation, and their customers for investing in our nation's future – this creates generational wealth for these children."

a5239.speaker: Sethaba Phalatsi, representing the Principal Secretary for Social Development
a5239.name: Sethaba Phalatsi
a5239.title: representing the Principal Secretary for Social Development
a5239.speech: welcomed the aid: "We are happy for the Ministry of Education, which needed this financial assistance more than ever following the recent crisis involving US government funding."

a5239.speaker: Dennis Plaatjies, Econet Telecom Lesotho CEO
a5239.name: Dennis Plaatjies
a5239.title: Econet Telecom Lesotho CEO
a5239.speech: viewed the donation as "more than a cheque, but a bridge of hope" and credited Econet's customers: "At ETL, we see ourselves not as the source, but as the bridge made possible by households and businesses across Lesotho. Every airtime recharge, subscription, and Eco-Cash transaction empowers us to show up where it matters most. Because of you, we bridge the gap between hardship and hope."

a5239.speaker: Dennis Plaatjies, Econet Telecom Lesotho CEO
a5239.name: Dennis Plaatjies
a5239.title: Econet Telecom Lesotho CEO
a5239.speech: highlighted the organisations' sustained commitment to education, revealing a combined M8.2 million investment in the past financial year, including the Moshoeshoe I Scholarship, which will soon welcome 10 new recipients, bringing the total to 40 scholars since its 2022 launch ; "Education remains one of the most powerful tools to transform lives and nations... We are honoured to stand with the Ministry and partners to keep Basotho children in school."

a5239.speaker: Strive Masiyiwa, founder (quoted by Dennis Plaatjies)
a5239.name: Strive Masiyiwa
a5239.title: founder (quoted by Dennis Plaatjies)
a5239.speech: "Every child has greatness in them. Sometimes, all they need is a little push, a little hope, a little help."

a5247.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP)
a5247.name: World Food Programme (WFP)
a5247.speech: Is calling for urgent action to address "catastrophic" food insecurity in eastern DRC ; warns that its operations are seriously threatened by the lack of funding, and that without additional contributions it could be forced "to suspend food aid to about half of the people it currently assists" in the coming weeks, needing $433 million to maintain its assistance until October 2025.

a5247.speaker: Eric Perdison, WFP Regional Director for Eastern and Southern Africa
a5247.name: Eric Perdison
a5247.title: WFP Regional Director for Eastern and Southern Africa
a5247.speech: Stressed that the DRC remained "a forgotten crisis" despite the dramatic scale of the humanitarian situation: "We need all our partners to come together - at the local, national and international levels," he declared on Tuesday, arguing for strengthened coordination between local authorities and humanitarian actors ; "People are generally living on a knife's edge," he warned, citing escalating conflicts, collapse of livelihoods, soaring prices, disrupted markets and limited access to humanitarian aid ; "I think the world is not reacting to the reality of the DRC the way it does for other emergencies," he lamented, arguing that the international community must step up its efforts to avoid a humanitarian collapse ; described the displacement crisis as "another historic record," with 7.8 million people uprooted across the country.

a5247.speaker: United Nations report (published last March)
a5247.name: United Nations report (published last March)
a5247.speech: Revealed that 28 million people are currently facing acute hunger in the country, and that in eastern DRC more than 10 million people in Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu and Tanganyika provinces are in severe food insecurity.

a5318.speaker: People desperate to flee Palma (anonymous, told the BBC)
a5318.name: People desperate to flee Palma (anonymous
a5318.title: told the BBC)
a5318.speech: Told the BBC that they have had to pay bribes to leave after security forces set up roadblocks, trapping thousands.

a5318.speaker: Farida, displaced woman from Palma (name changed)
a5318.name: Farida
a5318.title: displaced woman from Palma (name changed)
a5318.speech: "We stayed for 10 days in the woods" ; said her husband managed to raise 5,000 meticals ($80; £60) to get her and their children put on a list for departure and then onto a plane out, although the emergency flights are meant to be free: "At the beginning they didn't charge pregnant women, sick and children. Then they started carrying people who were on the list."

a5318.speaker: Witnesses to the Palma attack
a5318.name: Witnesses to the Palma attack
a5318.speech: Talk of seeing Palma's streets strewn with beheaded bodies, while some of the dead had also been hacked to pieces.

a5318.speaker: Total (the company)
a5318.name: Total (the company)
a5318.speech: According to the company, some 23,000 people had reached their gates by early April.

a5318.speaker: United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) (April assessment report)
a5318.name: United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) (April assessment report)
a5318.speech: Found 11,104 people living in the compound of EPC de Quitunda, a school close to the gas installation; the report says the "internally displaced persons are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance. Thirty per cent of the households are currently sleeping outdoors, whilst the remaining 70% currently live in makeshift shelter."

a5318.speaker: Hadijah, displaced woman from Palma (name changed)
a5318.name: Hadijah
a5318.title: displaced woman from Palma (name changed)
a5318.speech: Admits to paying 5,000 meticals to board an army flight: "We had no money and we were hungry and the children were sick. To leave Quitunda, I spoke to my husband and he spoke to his boss, who sent us the money via M-Pesa [mobile money transfer]." ; The two women say that there are many more left behind unable to leave, including Farida's husband.

a5318.speaker: Human Rights Watch (HRW)
a5318.name: Human Rights Watch (HRW)
a5318.speech: Says it's also spoken to people who admit to paying bribes to board evacuation flights or to get onto boats to leave Quitunda.

a5318.speaker: Zenaida Machado, senior Human Rights Watch researcher
a5318.name: Zenaida Machado
a5318.title: senior Human Rights Watch researcher
a5318.speech: "Can you imagine people that have no food, nothing to buy, that have lost everything during this conflict being forced to use the last money they have to be able to board their relatives onto a plane and be taken to safety?"

a5318.speaker: Mozambique's ministry of defence
a5318.name: Mozambique's ministry of defence
a5318.speech: The BBC approached the ministry about the allegations that displaced people are having to pay bribes to flee Palma, but it has not responded.

a5318.speaker: Two global aid agencies (anonymous)
a5318.name: Two global aid agencies (anonymous)
a5318.speech: Told us they could not speak on the record because they did not want to jeopardise delicate negotiations with the government.

a5318.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP)
a5318.name: World Food Programme (WFP)
a5318.speech: Says it is working with the government to ensure the right security conditions on the ground.

a5318.speaker: Pierre Lucas, acting WFP country director
a5318.name: Pierre Lucas
a5318.title: acting WFP country director
a5318.speech: "There are people in urgent need of humanitarian assistance in Palma and Quitunda" ; "WFP requires safe humanitarian access to reach the people most in need. There is a situation probably on the ground that is still dynamic and my understanding is that it's a work in progress."

a5318.speaker: Humanitarian workers based in Pemba (anonymous)
a5318.name: Humanitarian workers based in Pemba (anonymous)
a5318.speech: Have told the BBC they are worried about the lack of medical support in Quitunda as the only clinic is barely functioning.

a5322.speaker: Civil society organisations (CSOs) working on HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria
a5322.name: Civil society organisations (CSOs) working on HIV/AIDS
a5322.title: tuberculosis and malaria
a5322.speech: Have called for coordinated efforts to mobilise domestic resources and reduce Nigeria’s reliance on foreign donors.

a5322.speaker: Queen Ogbuji-Ladipo, Board Chair of Stop TB Partnership Nigeria
a5322.name: Queen Ogbuji-Ladipo
a5322.title: Board Chair of Stop TB Partnership Nigeria
a5322.speech: Stressed the urgent need for CSOs to unify efforts across disease programmes and take the lead in domestic resource advocacy; said it is very pertinent that Nigeria takes ownership of its health financing by moving beyond overreliance on government and external donors, warning that inconsistent funding cannot sustain Nigeria’s fight against infectious diseases ; “We cannot continue to depend indefinitely on the government or on donors. We need to harmonise the existing strategic plans of TB, HIV, and malaria and drive a collective advocacy for sustainable funding.” ; warned against operating in silos, urging CSOs to become a singular, credible voice that represents vulnerable communities at all levels of government ; acknowledged that foreign donors are stepping back due to economic pressures and fatigue, placing more responsibility on national actors.

a5322.speaker: Ayo Ipinmoye, National Coordinator of ACOMIN and Vice-Chair of Nigeria’s Country Coordinating Mechanism for the Global Fund
a5322.name: Ayo Ipinmoye
a5322.title: National Coordinator of ACOMIN and Vice-Chair of Nigeria’s Country Coordinating Mechanism for the Global Fund
a5322.speech: Urged civil society actors to move beyond dependence on foreign aid and take full ownership of Nigeria’s health outcomes; noted that for too long, CSOs have relied on donor funding to implement critical health interventions, while overlooking the importance of building domestic financial systems ; “Civil society must play its role in holding government and partners accountable. Health is a national responsibility that cannot be outsourced. As partners pull back globally, now is the time to take ownership of our health financing.” ; highlighted the trend of donor fatigue as foreign donors are starting to question the effectiveness of continuous aid ; “When donors keep putting money into malaria, TB, HIV, and the results are stagnant, they begin to think that it’s high time these countries start funding themselves.” ; stressed the importance of behaviour change and accountability at the grassroots level, pointing to poor utilisation of donor-funded resources like mosquito nets as a key failure point.

a5322.speaker: Ibrahim Tajudeen, Executive Secretary of Nigeria’s Country Coordinating Mechanism for the Global Fund
a5322.name: Ibrahim Tajudeen
a5322.title: Executive Secretary of Nigeria’s Country Coordinating Mechanism for the Global Fund
a5322.speech: Stressed that Nigeria must meet its co-financing commitments in order to continue accessing funding from international donors; noted that one of the Global Fund’s key requirements is for countries to provide at least 15 per cent counterpart funding for HIV, TB, and malaria programmes ; “Nigeria has struggled to meet this threshold in the past, and progress has only come when civil society organisations have stepped in to support the mobilisation of resources at the subnational level.” ; “It’s been a rough road getting to 15 per cent co-financing. The few times we made progress, it was because of partnerships – with states, and especially with civil society.” ; called for civil society actors to consolidate their strategies across disease areas rather than operate in fragmented silos, emphasising that harmonisation would enable better scale, reach, and efficiency; noted that integrated CSO efforts would allow local governments to benefit uniformly from advocacy and resource mobilisation efforts.

a5322.speaker: Ibrahim Tajudeen, Executive Secretary of Nigeria’s Country Coordinating Mechanism for the Global Fund
a5322.name: Ibrahim Tajudeen
a5322.title: Executive Secretary of Nigeria’s Country Coordinating Mechanism for the Global Fund
a5322.speech: Noted that current funding for malaria interventions is significantly below what is needed, with a shortfall of more than $1 billion, leaving millions without access to prevention and treatment ; “The malaria strategic plan alone is over $2 billion a year and we are facing a deficit of more than $1 billion. We know what’s needed and the issue now is how to fill that gap with real domestic resources.” ; noted that CSOs must not only advocate for funding but also monitor how funds are allocated and utilised to ensure they serve their intended purpose.

a5411.speaker: USAID and the Government of Tanzania (“Holela-Holela Itakukosti” national campaign)
a5411.name: USAID and the Government of Tanzania (“Holela-Holela Itakukosti” national campaign)
a5411.speech: Are reminding citizens to take responsibility and to remove obstacles in order to win the war against the danger of rabies.

a5411.speaker: Abdul Mhinte, Deputy Permanent Secretary, Tanzanian Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries
a5411.name: Abdul Mhinte
a5411.title: Deputy Permanent Secretary, Tanzanian Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries
a5411.speech: Stressed the importance of education for the community and of vaccination strategies in fighting the disease, and urged the strengthening of cooperation between public health officials and local communities in order to strengthen the joint response ; “Rabies can be prevented. Our goal is to ensure that every dog in Tanzania is vaccinated, and that every citizen knows what to do if they are bitten by a dog. Every community must take its part in this war.”

a5411.speaker: Revina, mother of three from Mwanza
a5411.name: Revina
a5411.title: mother of three from Mwanza
a5411.speech: “Before the campaign, I did not know the danger of rabies. When we learned that our dogs should be vaccinated, we took action immediately. Now, I have peace of mind letting my children play outside.”

a5469.speaker: A close friend of the author (unnamed)
a5469.name: A close friend of the author (unnamed)
a5469.speech: Recently reached out, expressing his frustration over our mutual friend, who, for some time now, has ignored his calls and messages.

a5469.speaker: Psychologists
a5469.name: Psychologists
a5469.speech: Adult friendships, according to psychologists, are shaped by three key factors: proximity, energy, and timing.

a5469.speaker: Leon Festinger and other psychologists
a5469.name: Leon Festinger and other psychologists
a5469.speech: Have studied this phenomenon, concluding that physical and emotional proximity fosters stronger, more resilient relationships.

a5522.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5522.name: Donald Trump
a5522.title: US President
a5522.speech: Speaking at a Nato summit in The Hague, said the strikes led to the “virtual obliteration” of Iran’s nuclear capabilities and set its atomic programme back “by decades” ; initially acknowledged some uncertainty, saying the intelligence on the attack was “very inconclusive”, but then said “it was very severe, it was [an] obliteration” ; likened the strikes to America’s atomic bombing of Hiroshima: “I don’t want to use an example of Hiroshima, I don’t want to use an example of Nagasaki, but that was essentially the same thing – that ended a war.”

a5522.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5522.name: Donald Trump
a5522.title: US President
a5522.speech: Asked if the US would strike again should Iran resume its nuclear activities, said: “Sure, but I’m not going to have to worry about that. It’s gone for years.”

a5522.speaker: Pete Hegseth, US Defence Secretary
a5522.name: Pete Hegseth
a5522.title: US Defence Secretary
a5522.speech: Said the preliminary Pentagon assessment was made with “low confidence” and the FBI was investigating the leak ; said the leak was politically motivated and insisted the bombs landed “precisely where they were supposed to” ; “Any assessment that tells you it was something otherwise is speculating with other motives” ; characterised the leak as “completely false”.

a5522.speaker: Sources familiar with the initial report (anonymous)
a5522.name: Sources familiar with the initial report (anonymous)
a5522.speech: Told the BBC’s US partner CBS that Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium was not eliminated; added that the strikes had only set the country’s nuclear programme back by a few months ; according to sources familiar with it, Iran’s centrifuges remain largely “intact” with the destruction limited to aboveground buildings; entrances to two nuclear facilities were blocked and some infrastructure was damaged, they said, but much of the deeper installations survived the blasts.

a5522.speaker: The White House
a5522.name: The White House
a5522.speech: Swiftly described the assessment as “flat-out wrong”.

a5522.speaker: Leaked Defense Intelligence Agency report
a5522.name: Leaked Defense Intelligence Agency report
a5522.speech: According to the report, strikes on the heavily fortified enrichment facilities at Fordo and Natanz had sealed off entrances but failed to destroy underground structures; the preliminary assessment also indicated that some of Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile had been moved prior to the attack.

a5522.speaker: Officials familiar with the leaked Defense Intelligence Agency evaluation (anonymous)
a5522.name: Officials familiar with the leaked Defense Intelligence Agency evaluation (anonymous)
a5522.speech: Warned it was an early assessment that could change as more information becomes available about the sites.

a5522.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a5522.name: Marco Rubio
a5522.title: US Secretary of State
a5522.speech: Cast doubt on the leaked report’s credibility, suggesting the contents had been distorted in the media and labelling the leakers as “professional stabbers”.

a5522.speaker: Gen Dan Caine, chairman of the joint chiefs of staff
a5522.name: Gen Dan Caine
a5522.title: chairman of the joint chiefs of staff
a5522.speech: Told reporters that it would take time to assess the damage to the facilities, but added that “all three sites sustained extremely severe damage and destruction”.

a5522.speaker: Hassan Abedini, deputy political director of Iran’s state broadcaster
a5522.name: Hassan Abedini
a5522.title: deputy political director of Iran’s state broadcaster
a5522.speech: Said the three sites targeted by the US had been evacuated a “while ago”, and that Iran “didn’t suffer a major blow because the materials had already been taken out”.

a5522.speaker: Tehran (Iranian government)
a5522.name: Tehran (Iranian government)
a5522.speech: Has always said its nuclear programme is for peaceful purposes.

a5522.speaker: US and Israeli officials
a5522.name: US and Israeli officials
a5522.speech: Have hailed the mission as a success.

a5534.speaker: Notícias (newspaper report)
a5534.name: Notícias (newspaper report)
a5534.speech: Reports today that the Council of Ministers yesterday approved regulations concerning the leader of the opposition, instituted through Law number 33/2014 of 30 December.

a5534.speaker: Armindo Tiago, Minister of Health of Mozambique
a5534.name: Armindo Tiago
a5534.title: Minister of Health of Mozambique
a5534.speech: Explained at the scheduled post-session press conference that only the evolution of the coronavirus in Mozambique would determine the extension or not of the state of emergency decreed on April 1 by the President of the Republic, and scheduled to end on 30 April: “Besides, it is not up to the Ministry of Health to decide on this. One thing is certain: many factors will be considered in taking this decision, especially the number of cases and the effective implementation of preventative measures so that we do not have more people infected.”

a5618.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a5618.title: Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.speech: On the AES-Russia consultations in Moscow: “We are here in Moscow with our colleagues, the foreign ministers of Burkina Faso and also of Niger, at the invitation of our Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov, in the framework of consultations between the Confederation of Sahel States and Russia, in this confederal format... The consultations showed that Russia and the AES countries share a common vision of their international engagement, an engagement based on respect for the sovereignty of our countries, respect for the sovereign choices of our countries, but also taking into account the interests of our populations, based also on the fact that our countries work at the international level to ensure that their voice is heard in order to fight together against imperialism, neocolonialism, the subjugation of our countries, the instrumentalisation of human rights... the rejection of interference in the internal affairs of countries” ; said the three pillars of the partnership are peace and security (including Russian support for joint military operations and a future unified AES force), diplomacy (allowing the countries to speak with one voice, with Russia as a permanent Security Council member), and development (economic integration, railways, roads, energy, agriculture, mining and an investment bank generating the AES's own resources); said the sides agreed to institutionalise the consultation mechanism, meeting at least once a year, alternating between Russia and the AES space, with the next meeting hosted in the AES space early next year.

a5618.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a5618.title: Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.speech: On a possible AES-Russia summit: said it is not something excluded a priori and was not openly discussed, but the mechanism is there and, depending on the guidance of the heads of state, it is possible they will reach that level; said the ministers, with Sergei Lavrov, and the ambassadors will continue the political consultation to obtain concrete results “in a spirit of a win-win partnership with Russia.”

a5618.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a5618.title: Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.speech: On arms autonomy and Russian assistance: said the countries wish to strengthen their capacities and develop autonomy “so that we get out of patterns of dependence”; said the acquisition of military equipment will be an ever-growing need and the countries will not simply continue importing it; said that with the Russian partner, who is not opposed to it, technology transfer and the strengthening of transformation capacities are envisaged, that President Goita has the ambition to develop a military industry in Mali, and that creating a military industry in the AES space would reduce dependence on imports, create jobs and advance industrialisation and structural transformation of the economies.

a5618.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a5618.title: Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.speech: On the common visa policy and the AES passport: said the visa question is an initiative of the heads of state, that experts have analysed it and made proposals, and that the project is under way on the ministers' table; said the AES passport, along with the AES biometric identity card, was adopted in January by Burkina, Mali and Niger, contains technical specifications that go beyond what ICAO normally requires, and was notified to ICAO and to all states concerned with physical specimens; said “To date we have not recorded any rejection of this passport by any country”, that many countries are progressively accepting it, and “I assure you that this passport meets the highest standards of security and reliability.”

a5618.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a5618.title: Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.speech: On the 0.5% confederal levy: said the levy is not new, the same mechanism having been used by ECOWAS for its financing, and that now the countries are no longer ECOWAS members the resources are redirected to finance the Confederation's functioning, institutions such as the investment bank, and structuring projects; said it reflects the heads of state's vision that “we do not establish them in order to ask external partners to finance them, which in the end authorises them to control our organisations and dictate their agenda” and that “We must count on ourselves.”

a5618.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a5618.title: Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.speech: On fiscal policy and development financing: said that as a matter of principle the countries and their citizens must be ready to assume greater financial responsibilities; said that because of wars, tensions and geopolitical considerations, resources for financing development or humanitarian action are becoming ever scarcer, and it will be up to the countries to identify innovative sources of financing or mobilise more internal resources, in a systemic approach to development financing.

a5618.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a5618.title: Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.speech: On the withdrawal from the OIF and relations with France: said calling it a cultural break “is going too far”, that historical ties with France exist though linked to colonisation; said speaking French is a colonial legacy and that in leaving the OIF the countries did not cut themselves off from French-speaking countries but left “an organisation that is under the influence of one particular country that promotes this language”; said the main reason for withdrawal was the organisation's “double-standards policy”, treating the same situations differently depending on whether a country has a calm or tense relationship with France: “We cannot be in an organisation and be treated differently, especially on the basis of political or geopolitical considerations, or because these decisions are remote-controlled by a country that has tensions or difficulties with us.”

a5618.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a5618.title: Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.speech: On national languages and Russian language cooperation: said French is a working language under Mali's new constitution while national languages now have official-language status, and that promoting national languages is a political objective and high priority, with President Goita having declared this the year of culture; welcomed the idea of Russian experts working with the AES countries to promote local languages as “a laudable objective”; said cultural relations with Russia date from the first years of independence, with thousands of Malians speaking Russian, and that learning Russian as a working language would foster exchanges and mutual understanding.

a5618.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a5618.title: Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.speech: On the halt to USAID: “Personally, I am not destabilised by this decision.
