Moreover, the government of Mali is not destabilised either” ; said that for several months Mali had been in very difficult discussions with USAID that ended in deadlock, “because the way American aid was dispensed in Mali did not allow Malians to choose the priorities, did not allow Malians to choose the NGOs that are selected for its implementation, and the resources in question did not even pass through the state budget”, a question on which Mali objected out of concern for national ownership ; said the second lesson is that “the aid was not coming for our populations, but... aid is a political instrument or an instrument of foreign policy to achieve a number of objectives” ; said the third lesson is that countries must be realistic, that such aid is bound to dry up, and that mechanisms must be found to finance countries from internal resources and from international resources “that do not necessarily obey these political diktats”, such as frameworks within the BRICS ; “Today it is USAID, yesterday it was Sweden in Mali's case, tomorrow it will be another country. So these are not isolated incidents, it is part of a dynamic.”

a5618.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.name: Abdoulaye Diop
a5618.title: Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a5618.speech: On the Russia-Ukraine ceasefire and wheat exports: said peace between Russia and Ukraine “will be beneficial for the whole world, for stability but also for the world economy, the economy of our countries” and that Mali supports it and encourages Russia's efforts; said “Mali marks its solidarity with Russia, as the AES also marks its solidarity with Russia in this struggle”; said Mali, which has broken off relations with Ukraine, considers Ukraine a terrorist state “insofar as Ukraine has openly called for and claimed support for terrorist groups in the Sahel and particularly in Mali, which has caused the death of many of our soldiers and of Malian citizens”, and that Ukraine must assume its responsibilities and be treated by African peoples as a troublemaker; said Mali and the AES favour all initiatives leading to peace, “but a just and lasting peace, a peace that takes into account Russia's security concerns.”

a5960.speaker: French Development Agency (AFD)
a5960.name: French Development Agency (AFD)
a5960.speech: Provides a good definition of Official Development Assistance on its website.

a5960.speaker: United Nations
a5960.name: United Nations
a5960.speech: Decided in 1970 that developed countries should devote 0.7% of their GDP to ODA; in 1986 proclaimed the inalienable right to development.

a5960.speaker: OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC)
a5960.name: OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC)
a5960.speech: Recommended in 2001 that ODA be untied.

a5960.speaker: OECD
a5960.name: OECD
a5960.speech: Reports that total global ODA reached 204 billion USD in 2022, up 24 billion USD on 2021, i.e. 0.33% to 0.36% of the GDP of advanced countries, far from the target set in 1970 by the UN; and that assistance allocated to infrastructure and productive sectors now accounts for no more than 30% of total ODA spending.

a5960.speaker: Paul Krugman, American Nobel laureate in economics (New York Times article “The trouble with Trade”, 2007)
a5960.name: Paul Krugman
a5960.title: American Nobel laureate in economics (New York Times article “The trouble with Trade”, 2007)
a5960.speech: Denounced the perverse effects of a globalisation focused on the search for the lowest production costs.

a5960.speaker: Jonathan Glennie, international expert (book “The trouble with aid”, 2012)
a5960.name: Jonathan Glennie
a5960.title: international expert (book “The trouble with aid”, 2012)
a5960.speech: Argued for a progressive reduction of dependence on international aid.

a5960.speaker: French parliamentary report of 2024 (National Assembly)
a5960.name: French parliamentary report of 2024 (National Assembly)
a5960.speech: Describes ODA as “illegible, costly and ineffective”, pointing to its integration into an “invasive” multilateral whole and to financial commitments deemed worrying, and judges it “insufficiently effective and of little service to French interests”; refers to a “black hole of European ODA”.

a5960.speaker: Office of Inspector General for USAID (OIG-USAID) audit
a5960.name: Office of Inspector General for USAID (OIG-USAID) audit
a5960.speech: Concluded that USAID had a limited view of international organisations’ ability to safeguard American funds (which rose from 5.6 billion USD in 2019 to 21.4 billion USD in 2022, +282%), that USAID did not conduct an organisational capacity review for 70% of them and did not put in place follow-up to its recommendations, and that in 2025 it still has problems obtaining information from these organisations on fraud, corruption or other offences.

a5960.speaker: French Cour des Comptes (report of June 2023)
a5960.name: French Cour des Comptes (report of June 2023)
a5960.speech: Described a situation for French ODA close to that found by the USAID Inspector General.

a5960.speaker: UK House of Lords report (2022)
a5960.name: UK House of Lords report (2022)
a5960.speech: Noted a 21% drop in British ODA between 2020 and 2021, with ODA moving from 0.7% of GDP to 0.5%.

a5960.speaker: US Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
a5960.name: US Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
a5960.speech: Announced on 3 February 2025 the closure of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), a key actor in international ODA, which in 2024 accounted for more than 40 billion USD of global ODA.

a5960.speaker: USAID (statement on its website)
a5960.name: USAID (statement on its website)
a5960.speech: “On Friday, February 7, 2025, at 11:59 pm (EST) all USAID direct hire personnel will be placed on administrative leave globally, with the exception of designated personnel responsible for mission-critical functions, core leadership and specially designated programs... The Agency will consider case-by-case exceptions and return travel extensions based on personal or family hardship, mobility or safety concerns, or other reasons... Thank you for your service.”

a5960.speaker: UN agencies (UNDP, WFP) and international organisations (World Bank, IMF)
a5960.name: UN agencies (UNDP
a5960.title: WFP) and international organisations (World Bank, IMF)
a5960.speech: Consider ODA indispensable for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals and as a lever for reducing inequalities and promoting equitable human development.

a5960.speaker: Think tanks (ODA detractors)
a5960.name: Think tanks (ODA detractors)
a5960.speech: Argue that ODA creates dependencies and generates no real and lasting economic progress.

a5960.speaker: Civil society organisations and local voices in recipient countries
a5960.name: Civil society organisations and local voices in recipient countries
a5960.speech: Criticise ODA for ineffectiveness, waste, misappropriation, corruption, interference, unsuitability to local realities, neocolonialism and domination.

a5960.speaker: World Bank
a5960.name: World Bank
a5960.speech: Reports that world GDP rose from 1,364.5 billion USD in 1950 to 105,435 billion USD in 2023, a multiplication by 77 in nominal terms.

a5960.speaker: A major industrialist (unnamed)
a5960.name: A major industrialist (unnamed)
a5960.speech: “One must remain the owner of one’s aid.”

a5960.speaker: Daniel Alystair (author of the chronicle, with thanks to Mamadou Sinsy Coulibaly, former President of the National Council of Employers of Mali)
a5960.name: Daniel Alystair (author of the chronicle
a5960.title: with thanks to Mamadou Sinsy Coulibaly, former President of the National Council of Employers of Mali)
a5960.speech: Argues that ODA is at a turning point and that its in-depth reform, rather than its abolition, is imperative: redirecting ODA towards genuinely transformative projects (infrastructure, industrialisation, in-situ processing, basic and technical education, economic empowerment), making development banks autonomous, concentrating donor ODA on earmarked bilateral projects with evaluations, and giving a major role to the private sector; writes that ODA, principally State-run and transiting through structures with weak governance, “has historically failed”, and that the closure of USAID “can (must) also be interpreted as a first step towards a necessary reorganisation - American, then global - of international aid.”

a6082.speaker: Four sources familiar with the plan (anonymous)
a6082.name: Four sources familiar with the plan (anonymous)
a6082.speech: Told Reuters on Thursday that President Donald Trump's administration plans to keep fewer than 300 staff at the U.S. Agency for International Development out of the agency's worldwide total of more than 10,000, and that only 294 staff at the agency would be allowed to keep their jobs, including only 12 in the Africa bureau and eight in the Asia bureau.

a6082.speaker: J. Brian Atwood, former head of USAID, now a senior fellow at Brown University's Watson Institute
a6082.name: J. Brian Atwood
a6082.title: former head of USAID, now a senior fellow at Brown University's Watson Institute
a6082.speech: “That's outrageous,” adding the mass termination of personnel would effectively kill an agency that has helped keep tens of millions of people around the world from dying ; “A lot of people will not survive.”

a6082.speaker: U.S. Department of State
a6082.name: U.S. Department of State
a6082.speech: Did not respond to a request for comment.

a6082.speaker: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State and acting USAID administrator
a6082.name: Marco Rubio
a6082.title: Secretary of State and acting USAID administrator
a6082.speech: Had said the administration was identifying and designating programs that would be exempted from the sweeping stop-work orders, which have threatened efforts around the globe to stop the spread of disease, prevent famine and otherwise alleviate poverty.

a6082.speaker: Sources familiar with events at the agency (anonymous)
a6082.name: Sources familiar with events at the agency (anonymous)
a6082.speech: Said on Thursday that some workers had begun receiving termination notices.

a6082.speaker: USAID website (official notice)
a6082.name: USAID website (official notice)
a6082.speech: Said that as of midnight on Friday, February 7, “all USAID direct hire personnel will be placed on administrative leave globally, with the exception of designated personnel responsible for mission-critical functions, core leadership and specially designated programs”; it said essential personnel expected to continue working would be informed by Thursday at 3 p.m. EST.

a6082.speaker: Congressional Research Service (CRS) report
a6082.name: Congressional Research Service (CRS) report
a6082.speech: According to the CRS, USAID employed more than 10,000 people around the world, two-thirds of them outside the United States, and managed more than $40 billion in fiscal 2023; the agency provided aid to some 130 countries in 2023, the top recipients being Ukraine, followed by Ethiopia, Jordan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Somalia, Yemen and Afghanistan.

a6377.speaker: Kayode Ojewale (the late writer, quoted by his father)
a6377.name: Kayode Ojewale (the late writer
a6377.title: quoted by his father)
a6377.speech: Would query him: "Dad, what's going on? I haven't seen you write lately."

a6377.speaker: Kayode Ojewale (the late writer)
a6377.name: Kayode Ojewale (the late writer)
a6377.speech: Would cut a young person down to size by pointing to an elderly woman and announcing, "Young man, hope you know that woman over there was the one who circumcised you!"

a6377.speaker: Kayode Ojewale, "Asamabiri: A Youth Corps Member's Experience" (unpublished book)
a6377.name: Kayode Ojewale
a6377.title: "Asamabiri: A Youth Corps Member's Experience" (unpublished book)
a6377.speech: Its conclusion foresaw the food crisis now pillaging the land and recommended a strategic solution: "Asamabiri can...be the food basket of the Niger Delta if the authorities harness its agricultural products. Its potential is enormous, waiting to be tapped to the full realities of full economic activity and industry. Government and the private sector must join hands to move into Asamabiri and turn the area into a developed and prosperous region. This way we can truly talk of diversifying the Nigerian economy and freeing it from dependence on oil."

a6377.speaker: Editors of a business newspaper in Lagos
a6377.name: Editors of a business newspaper in Lagos
a6377.speech: Reckoned that pinning the prolific contributor exclusively to their desk might be more profitable to the paper than having him shared with others in the industry.

a6377.speaker: Bunmi, Kayode Ojewale's wife (a professional nurse)
a6377.name: Bunmi
a6377.title: Kayode Ojewale's wife (a professional nurse)
a6377.speech: Called on Wednesday 4 July, 2024 to say that Kayode was gravely down with cough and unsettling breathing issues, and told him she was taking her husband to a private hospital in their neighbourhood at Alakuko, Lagos; when his condition deteriorated there, she suggested a switch to Olabisi Onabanjo University Teaching Hospital (OOUTH), Sagamu, where she had worked and was fully convinced her husband would receive much better care.

a6377.speaker: Colleagues, childhood friends and LAUTECH schoolmates of Kayode Ojewale
a6377.name: Colleagues
a6377.title: childhood friends and LAUTECH schoolmates of Kayode Ojewale
a6377.speech: Have offered profuse eulogies of endearment, saying affable Kayode touched their lives not only on the campus but also away from its environment; they fondly referred to him as Professor, "because he had the carriage of a Prof."

a6377.speaker: One of Kayode Ojewale's friends (unnamed)
a6377.name: One of Kayode Ojewale's friends (unnamed)
a6377.speech: Said Kayode led him into writing for the media.

a6377.speaker: One of Kayode Ojewale's closest pals (unnamed)
a6377.name: One of Kayode Ojewale's closest pals (unnamed)
a6377.speech: Said their late friend was the one who always checked on them, one by one, and reminded them to felicitate with each other on their birthdays.

a6377.speaker: Dapo Olorunyomi, publisher of Premium Times
a6377.name: Dapo Olorunyomi
a6377.title: publisher of Premium Times
a6377.speech: Would always refer to Kayode as Old Man, dropping Kayus.

a6640.speaker: Mike Lee, US Senator (Disengaging Entirely from the United Nations Debacle / DEFUND Act bill)
a6640.name: Mike Lee
a6640.title: US Senator (Disengaging Entirely from the United Nations Debacle / DEFUND Act bill)
a6640.speech: Introduced the "Disengaging Entirely from the United Nations Debacle (DEFUND Act)" bill, which proposes a complete withdrawal of the United States from the United Nations, invoking issues of national sovereignty, budgetary responsibility and presumed bias within the organisation.

a6640.speaker: Kofi Annan, former UN Secretary-General
a6640.name: Kofi Annan
a6640.title: former UN Secretary-General
a6640.speech: "When the United States does not engage, the whole world suffers."

a6640.speaker: Paul Kennedy, American historian
a6640.name: Paul Kennedy
a6640.title: American historian
a6640.speech: Described the UN as "the instrument through which America exports its vision of world order."

a6640.speaker: Supporters of the DEFUND Act
a6640.name: Supporters of the DEFUND Act
a6640.speech: Consider that continued US involvement in the UN undermines national sovereignty and weighs on the American taxpayer, arguing that the world organisation has deviated from its primary mission of promoting peace and security and has instead become a platform for anti-Americanism and a forum in which non-democratic regimes exercise excessive influence ; argue that the UN General Assembly grants equal voting rights to all member states regardless of population size or political system, so that small and/or authoritarian states have the same voting power as large democracies, and that these states tend to display ostracism and hostility towards the United States and its allies, particularly Israel ; consider that the UN undermines American sovereignty by imposing international norms that contradict US values or interests, and that certain UN resolutions on climate change and human rights constitute interference in American domestic policy.

a6640.speaker: Boutros Boutros-Ghali, former UN Secretary-General
a6640.name: Boutros Boutros-Ghali
a6640.title: former UN Secretary-General
a6640.speech: "Diplomacy is not only about speaking, but about listening, understanding and adapting."

a6655.speaker: One of the pregnant women at the Ouedo health centre (unnamed)
a6655.name: One of the pregnant women at the Ouedo health centre (unnamed)
a6655.speech: "Look, it's as if you didn't even eat before coming back for your consultation," she called out to her neighbour whom she was trying to weigh.

a6655.speaker: Rose D, pregnant woman attending the group prenatal consultation
a6655.name: Rose D
a6655.title: pregnant woman attending the group prenatal consultation
a6655.speech: "Last time, my blood pressure went down to 8. I was a little tired and it was as if someone were hitting me in the neck."

a6655.speaker: Dr Faustin Onikpo, coordinator of the group prenatal consultation pilot
a6655.name: Dr Faustin Onikpo
a6655.title: coordinator of the group prenatal consultation pilot
a6655.speech: Said that group prenatal consultation (CPN-G) is a periodic assessment of the progress of the pregnancy from conception to delivery, with a view to preventing, or detecting and correcting in time, any abnormality ; "It makes it easier to teach the women in the group the essential things they need to know to stay healthy along with the babies they are carrying. They can assess each other's state of health before being seen individually, and more quickly, by the midwife. It thus gives the women in the group the opportunity to talk among themselves and look for solutions to anything that might prevent them from following the good practices taught and recommended."

a6655.speaker: Tranquiline Gnimagnon, pregnant woman attending for the first time
a6655.name: Tranquiline Gnimagnon
a6655.title: pregnant woman attending for the first time
a6655.speech: "I couldn't believe it when I was measuring the other women's blood pressure or when another woman weighed me. A trust develops. The discussions were open. The midwife welcomed us warmly. I personally gained a great deal in a short time. It is a kind of sharing of experiences."

a6655.speaker: Chimene Boton, pregnant woman attending for the second time
a6655.name: Chimene Boton
a6655.title: pregnant woman attending for the second time
a6655.speech: "I had come for a consultation when I was told about it. I did not hesitate to join the group. I immediately felt the good social atmosphere. We are having new experiences. I am able to measure blood pressure and to understand the warning signs a pregnant woman must watch out for."

a6655.speaker: Diane Akidocho, pregnant woman attending the group prenatal consultation
a6655.name: Diane Akidocho
a6655.title: pregnant woman attending the group prenatal consultation
a6655.speech: "We even have notions about the period after delivery. There are many things I did not know. When you are pregnant, you must take the tablets regularly, according to the instructions given. As for danger signs, I pay attention to headaches, bleeding, fatigue, fever, etc. Even for a woman who already has three children, there are new reflexes that you develop with this form of prenatal consultation."

a6655.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a6655.name: World Health Organization (WHO)
a6655.speech: According to WHO, prenatal care is a platform for delivering important health services, including health promotion, screening, diagnosis and disease prevention, and offers the opportunity to communicate with and support pregnant women, families and communities at a critical moment in these women's lives; WHO recommends that every pregnant woman make at least four antenatal visits and that the first take place in the first trimester of pregnancy.

a6655.speaker: Demographic and Health Survey of Benin (2017-2018)
a6655.name: Demographic and Health Survey of Benin (2017-2018)
a6655.speech: According to its results, the proportion of pregnant women in Benin who had at least four antenatal visits is 52% (59% urban, 48% rural); in rural areas the percentage of women with no antenatal follow-up is more than twice that in urban areas (14% against 6%); only one woman in two (51%) made her first antenatal visit in the first trimester (57% urban against 46% rural), and in 10% of cases women make their first visit at 6-7 months of pregnancy.

a6655.speaker: Dr Faustin Onikpo, coordinator of the group prenatal consultation pilot
a6655.name: Dr Faustin Onikpo
a6655.title: coordinator of the group prenatal consultation pilot
a6655.speech: Said there is evidence that CPN-G improves the use and coverage of the services offered during antenatal consultation, in particular coverage of the intermittent preventive treatment recommended against malaria in pregnancy, and that a baseline survey was carried out with a final survey due after 18 months of implementation ; "The final survey will provide material to the Ministry of Health, which will decide whether it is appropriate to scale up this CPN model in Benin."

a6655.speaker: Diane Akidocho, pregnant woman attending the group prenatal consultation
a6655.name: Diane Akidocho
a6655.title: pregnant woman attending the group prenatal consultation
a6655.speech: Argued for generalising the model: "It is going to help women a lot. It is not that I lack the means. But through exchanging with other women, it motivated me. With this atmosphere, there is no reason to miss consultations."

a6708.speaker: Tanzania's Ministry of Health
a6708.name: Tanzania's Ministry of Health
a6708.speech: Has pledged to continue collaborating with Amref to implement various projects aimed at empowering communities to address health challenges in the area of comprehensive prevention, care and treatment of HIV.

a6708.speaker: Dr John Jingu, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Health of Tanzania
a6708.name: Dr John Jingu
a6708.title: Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Health of Tanzania
a6708.speech: Said that the main agenda under President Samia Suluhu Hassan is to ensure that high-quality healthcare services reach every Tanzanian, noting that joint efforts were needed between the government and stakeholders including Amref in order to achieve the goal ; "We all agree that whenever there are health challenges such as disease outbreaks, they are largely driven by social determinants. Therefore, this issue must continue to be emphasised to ensure we achieve positive outcomes where everyone has access to healthcare services."

a6708.speaker: Dr John Jingu, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Health of Tanzania
a6708.name: Dr John Jingu
a6708.title: Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Health of Tanzania
a6708.speech: Said that after conducting an assessment of the discussions, it will help in project implementation ; "It will ensure that everyone has a shared understanding and knows the purpose of these projects, the challenges they face and how to address them."

a6708.speaker: Dr John Jingu, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Health of Tanzania
a6708.name: Dr John Jingu
a6708.title: Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Health of Tanzania
a6708.speech: Called upon stakeholders to ensure that other stakeholders and the private sector recognise the benefits of the interventions being implemented under the project ; "When other stakeholders see that the interventions in place will help them by reducing costs or increasing productivity, they will not hesitate to contribute where needed."

a6708.speaker: Dr John Jingu, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Health of Tanzania
a6708.name: Dr John Jingu
a6708.title: Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Health of Tanzania
a6708.speech: Commended Amref for taking a leading role in collaborating with the ministry to address various health challenges in the society ; "You have been key partners in building the capacity of healthcare providers to address health challenges, as this is a crucial tool in achieving universal health coverage."

a6807.speaker: Ben Nangombe, Executive Director of the Ministry of Health and Social Services (Namibia)
a6807.name: Ben Nangombe
a6807.title: Executive Director of the Ministry of Health and Social Services (Namibia)
a6807.speech: reiterated that Namibia has made commendable progress in curbing the spread of infectious diseases like HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria. "We have witnessed significant forward movement in achieving the goals articulated in the National Strategic Framework, thanks in large part to the invaluable support by our Development Cooperation Partners and the active role of Civil Society Organisations (CSOs). The data and figures towards Namibia's achievements of the UNAIDS 95-95-95 fast-tracked targets for HIV are well known to all of you. As of 2022 in Namibia, 94% of HIV-positive individuals know their status, 97% of them are on antiretroviral therapy (ART), and 93% have reached viral suppression (94-97-93)." ; "This is the last mile, and we dare not relent. We will not falter. Not now, when we have achieved so much. Let us maintain the momentum and deliver a solid NOP and a comprehensive sustainability framework to operationalise our NSF for HIV, TB, malaria, and hepatitis."

a6807.speaker: Cheryl Amoroso, PEPFAR Representative
a6807.name: Cheryl Amoroso
a6807.title: PEPFAR Representative
a6807.speech: discussed the funding perspective of PEPFAR as a donor. "From a PEPFAR perspective, we need to already embrace change to together understand the transformation of HIV programming in line with this developing vision that the country has for its future health system, not just from an HIV perspective but holistically. From a donor viewpoint, we are ready to adapt our investments to help realise this developing vision, which is why today and tomorrow are so important. We will use this roadmap to guide our investment. The Namibia PEPFAR investments have already started making shifts better aligned with the future vision that is already developing, and the clarity that we will have on this documentation will continue to support that transition."

a6839.speaker: Executive Director of DARE Organisation (unnamed)
a6839.name: Executive Director of DARE Organisation (unnamed)
a6839.speech: Highlighted the role of civil society in supporting government efforts to combat the spread of HIV: “Our institution works closely with communities to identify solutions to health-related challenges, particularly sexual and reproductive health and HIV. Today, we are focusing on the U=U concept if the virus is undetectable, it is untransmittable as a strategy to enhance accurate public knowledge and fight stigma” ; “We work closely with communities to co-create solutions to health challenges, including HIV and reproductive health. Today, our focus is on promoting the U=U concept, meaning that when a person living with HIV is on effective treatment and the virus becomes undetectable, they cannot transmit it sexually” ; stressed the need to deliver accurate information to the public to combat stigma, increase testing, and promote consistent use of antiretroviral therapy (ART).

a6839.speaker: Bahati Haule, DARE’s Advocacy officer
a6839.name: Bahati Haule
a6839.title: DARE’s Advocacy officer
a6839.speech: Spoke on the impact of funding challenges on HIV programmes: “With the recent suspension of some USAID-funded initiatives, many civil society organisations have had to pause community-based services. However, we are hopeful because some programmes may continue under waiver arrangements, depending on the selection process.”

a6839.speaker: Bahati Haule, DARE’s Advocacy officer
a6839.name: Bahati Haule
a6839.title: DARE’s Advocacy officer
a6839.speech: Added that stigma remains a key driver of new infections: “Our U=U programme provides education on testing and proper use of treatment. When people are supported to stay on medication and suppress their viral load, they can live full, healthy lives without transmitting the virus.”

a6839.speaker: A medical officer from a participating health centre (anonymous)
a6839.name: A medical officer from a participating health centre (anonymous)
a6839.speech: Highlighted the practical impact of such meetings: “We are the ones who deal directly with patients. These forums equip us with updated information we can share within our communities.”

a6839.speaker: Dr Tamari Tom, HIV advocate and social media influencer
a6839.name: Dr Tamari Tom
a6839.title: HIV advocate and social media influencer
a6839.speech: Shared her approach on how to share her knowledge with the community: “I use digital platforms and one-on-one conversations to share accurate HIV information. Many people still lack awareness of the importance of testing or staying on treatment, so this dialogue is critical for public health.”

a6839.speaker: Participants at the Dar es Salaam high-level dialogue
a6839.name: Participants at the Dar es Salaam high-level dialogue
a6839.speech: Called for stronger collaboration, continued funding, and community-led approaches to amplify the U=U message and reduce new infections.

a6850.speaker: Dangote Petroleum Refinery (statement issued by its management)
a6850.name: Dangote Petroleum Refinery (statement issued by its management)
a6850.speech: Denied importing finished petrol (PMS) with high sulphur content into Nigeria, describing the claims as false, malicious, and misleading, and clarified that the cargo in question is an intermediate feedstock, not finished petrol. Said, “As a world-scale complex refinery, Dangote processes a range of crude oils and intermediate feedstocks, a standard global practice aimed at optimising production and quality.” ; “The cargo in question is an intermediate feedstock, not finished petrol, and will be fully refined in our units to meet Nigerian and international quality standards.” ; “Operating within a Free Trade Zone, Dangote Petroleum Refinery refines and sells only high-quality fuels, compliant with all regulatory specifications. Our exports of petroleum products to the United States and Europe, among the world's most regulated markets, underscore our adherence to global benchmarks.”

a6850.speaker: Dangote Petroleum Refinery (management)
a6850.name: Dangote Petroleum Refinery (management)
a6850.speech: Added that all imports are accompanied by quality certificates, which are shared with regulators, and expressed willingness to make these documents publicly available to ensure transparency and accountability; reaffirmed the company’s commitment to “advancing Nigeria's energy independence, upholding the highest standards of quality and transparency, and delivering cleaner fuels for Nigeria and beyond”.

a6850.speaker: Certificate of Quality No. MFG-250923-00016 issued by Phillips 66 Limited, operators of the Humber Refinery (UK)
a6850.name: Certificate of Quality No. MFG-250923-00016 issued by Phillips 66 Limited
a6850.title: operators of the Humber Refinery (UK)
a6850.speech: Confirms that a consignment of High-Sulphur Catalytic Gasoline (FCC Gasoline) was loaded for shipment to Dangote Nigeria on September 21, 2025, and certifies that the sample analysed was a composite sample taken immediately after loading aboard the vessel Clearocean Marigold and tested at the refinery’s accredited laboratory in North Lincolnshire, UK. According to the report, the product appeared “clear and bright,” its density at 15 °C measured 0.7375 kilograms per litre, the boiling range spanned 49 °C to 155 °C, RON was 92.3 and MON 79.3, and vapour pressure was 33 kilopascals; the report highlights a very high sulphur concentration of 690 parts per million by weight, far exceeding the 50 ppm environmental limit imposed for retail fuels in many jurisdictions.

a6940.speaker: Anna Makakala, Commissioner General of Immigration (Tanzania)
a6940.name: Anna Makakala
a6940.title: Commissioner General of Immigration (Tanzania)
a6940.speech: Said the number of foreign nationals entering the country legally rose from 753,544 in 2023 to 870,193 between January and November 2024, an increase of 116,649 people, and said the increase resulted from the easing of return-visa conditions for some countries and cheaper permit fees for diaspora of Tanzanian origin when they arrive home ; "Migrants contribute to the investment sector; in the 2023/24 financial year up to November, a total of 20,979 residence permits have already been issued to foreign nationals who needed to enter or live in the country."

a6940.speaker: Anna Makakala, Commissioner General of Immigration (Tanzania)
a6940.name: Anna Makakala
a6940.title: Commissioner General of Immigration (Tanzania)
a6940.speech: Said that despite the good things migrants bring, irregular migration endangers the defence and security of the country and is linked to an increase in criminal acts including robbery, drug trafficking, prostitution, banditry, money laundering, the reduction of employment opportunities or of the basic rights of citizens, the erosion of morals, and terrorism; and said that because of these challenges the community and stakeholders have a duty to expose migrants who violate procedures so that government authorities can take action, to keep the country secure and to ensure the rights of those people are protected.

a6940.speaker: Anna Makakala, Commissioner General of Immigration (Tanzania)
a6940.name: Anna Makakala
a6940.title: Commissioner General of Immigration (Tanzania)
a6940.speech: Said the Immigration Department, in collaboration with the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and other institutions, from January to November 2024 removed 2,383 migrants from prison who had completed their sentences and returned them to their home countries.

a6940.speaker: Anna Makakala, Commissioner General of Immigration (Tanzania)
a6940.name: Anna Makakala
a6940.title: Commissioner General of Immigration (Tanzania)
a6940.speech: Appealed to parents and guardians to supervise their young people so that they are not deceived by employment agents or by study opportunities abroad and end up drawn into the illegal business of human trafficking, which has become rampant in the community ; urged citizens living abroad to live in accordance with the laws and procedures established, since the government is committed to providing good services to foreigners and to Tanzanians so as to bring about their personal development and that of the nation.

a6940.speaker: Maurizio Busatti, Head of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) in Tanzania
a6940.name: Maurizio Busatti
a6940.title: Head of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) in Tanzania
a6940.speech: Said that to achieve the dream of dignified, safe, orderly and accountable migration there must be work in unity, step by step ; "Migration is not only a process of change for an individual, but also for families, communities and even the whole nation. The United Republic of Tanzania has made great strides in better understanding migration issues through accurate statistics, knowing the number of migrants, who they are, where they are, and also how to take action against challenges such as the exploitation of migrants."

a6940.speaker: Maurizio Busatti, Head of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) in Tanzania
a6940.name: Maurizio Busatti
a6940.title: Head of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) in Tanzania
a6940.speech: Said that migrants often find themselves falling into the hands of dishonest people, and that this is where the important work of the Immigration Department becomes apparent; said that identifying, documenting and tracking national and third-country migrants is an important responsibility that contributes to ensuring dignified and orderly migration.

a6946.speaker: 'What We Know About Exit - Practical Guidance For Developing Exit Strategies in the Field', publication of the C-SAFE Regional Learning Spaces Initiative by Alison Gardner, Kara Greenblott and Erika Joubert
a6946.name: 'What We Know About Exit - Practical Guidance For Developing Exit Strategies in the Field'
a6946.title: publication of the C-SAFE Regional Learning Spaces Initiative by Alison Gardner, Kara Greenblott and Erika Joubert
a6946.speech: Outlined three basic approaches to Exit Strategies - 1) phasing down, 2) phasing out, and 3) phasing over - and grouped the criteria used to determine when to exit programs into three general categories: time limit, achievement of program impacts, and achievement of benchmarks; recommends implementing exit plans in a gradual, phased manner, since the staggered graduation of project sites can contribute to sustained outcomes by applying lessons learned from earlier sites to those that come later, and recommends continued contact with communities after phase over or phase out is complete to help support sustainability of outcomes.

a6946.speaker: 'What We Know About Exit - Practical Guidance For Developing Exit Strategies in the Field', publication of the C-SAFE Regional Learning Spaces Initiative by Alison Gardner, Kara Greenblott and Erika Joubert
a6946.name: 'What We Know About Exit - Practical Guidance For Developing Exit Strategies in the Field'
a6946.title: publication of the C-SAFE Regional Learning Spaces Initiative by Alison Gardner, Kara Greenblott and Erika Joubert
a6946.speech: Sets out the challenges to developing and implementing Exit Strategies and suggested remedies: recurrent droughts and floods, for which it recommends focusing on enhancing community resilience in disaster-prone areas and conducting risk assessments and action plans; funding and project cycles and the uncertainty of future funding, for which it suggests contingency plans for various funding scenarios including fundraising for complementary funding, ensuring the program is not 100% reliant on one donor, and keeping staff informed as plans change; belated planning of an Exit Strategy; lack of resources and funding restrictions; the need for training and improved understanding among staff; high turnover of staff and local partners; lack of volunteers and local partners to phase over to; the continued supply of inputs after exit; and limited follow-up capacity, for which it suggests a staggered exit, soliciting complementary funding for post-project follow-up, and a post-project evaluation several months later to assess whether activities and outcomes were sustainable.

a7102.speaker: Nesrdin Redwan, manager of the Sendelet Food Processing plant
a7102.name: Nesrdin Redwan
a7102.title: manager of the Sendelet Food Processing plant
a7102.speech: "We'll expand the number of employees to 80 when we start working in double shifts," adding that the plant expects to process guava and multi-fruit juice with carton packaging after undergoing an expansion.

a7102.speaker: Nesrdin Redwan, manager of the Sendelet Food Processing plant
a7102.name: Nesrdin Redwan
a7102.title: manager of the Sendelet Food Processing plant
a7102.speech: Said electric power outages and political unrest in the area were the main challenge that the owners of the company faced during the construction of the plant.

a7102.speaker: Nesrdin Redwan, manager of the Sendelet Food Processing plant
a7102.name: Nesrdin Redwan
a7102.title: manager of the Sendelet Food Processing plant
a7102.speech: "We also have a plan to export our products to neighbouring countries, including Djibouti and Sudan."

a7102.speaker: Hailemariam Kebede (PhD), lecturer at Addis Abeba University's School of Commerce
a7102.name: Hailemariam Kebede (PhD)
a7102.title: lecturer at Addis Abeba University's School of Commerce
a7102.speech: Recommends the management of the company consider decreasing the price of the product at least for six months to penetrate the market.

a7102.speaker: Hailemariam Kebede (PhD), lecturer at Addis Abeba University's School of Commerce
a7102.name: Hailemariam Kebede (PhD)
a7102.title: lecturer at Addis Abeba University's School of Commerce
a7102.speech: Says that the company should produce the raw material locally to save foreign currency: "If they didn't manufacture the raw material locally, it would be good to make a joint venture agreement with another company."

a7114.speaker: Mekuria Lemma, Strategy and Investment Director with the Ethiopian Electric Power (EEP)
a7114.name: Mekuria Lemma
a7114.title: Strategy and Investment Director with the Ethiopian Electric Power (EEP)
a7114.speech: Told Capital that the two bodies agreed on a feed in tariff in the beginning; said that EEP has agreed to pay USD 0.075 cents per kwh for the Corbetti project, and that the Tulu Moye and Abaya projects which will be developed in the second phase will contribute to Corbetti Geothermal to gain USD 0.069 cents per kwh: "They have a scale advantage on the Tulu Moye and Abaya projects so the price has also been reduced compared with Corbetti."

a7114.speaker: Mekuria Lemma, Strategy and Investment Director with the Ethiopian Electric Power (EEP)
a7114.name: Mekuria Lemma
a7114.title: Strategy and Investment Director with the Ethiopian Electric Power (EEP)
a7114.speech: Said that the first phase of the project that will take place at Corbetti will take 7.9 years and enable to generate 500 MW project; said that the power production will reach 500MW in the long run: "We will receive the first 20MW within two years and it will continue on its growth step by step."

a7114.speaker: EEP officials
a7114.name: EEP officials
a7114.speech: "A Geothermal energy project by its nature is not expected to be fully operational in a few years."

a7299.speaker: Members of Parliament (MPs) of Tanzania
a7299.name: Members of Parliament (MPs) of Tanzania
a7299.speech: Have expressed admiration for the USAID Tuhifadhi Maliasili Project (Preserve Natural Resources), a transformative initiative aimed at conserving Tanzania's natural resources. In a call to action, lawmakers urged the review of policies and laws to promote greater participation and inclusion of women, youth and marginalised groups in conservation activities.

a7299.speaker: Benedict Minja, MJUMITA Project Officer
a7299.name: Benedict Minja
a7299.title: MJUMITA Project Officer
a7299.speech: According to MJUMITA Project Officer, Benedict Minja, the project is being implemented in seven wildlife corridors namely: Amani-Nilo, Kwakuchinja, Nyerere-Selous Udzungwa, Ruaha Rungwa–Katavi, Ruaha Rungwa-Inyonga, Kigosi Moyowosi – Burigi Chato and Mahale – Katavi. “Through a Secure – Protect – Sustain approach, the project strengthens robust, locally led and inclusive approaches to biodiversity conservation, bringing together an effective combination of government, civil society and private sector actors throughout the country,’’ he said.

a7299.speaker: Beatrice Sendegeya, gender expert
a7299.name: Beatrice Sendegeya
a7299.title: gender expert
a7299.speech: “In partnership with USAID, we hope to renew economic benefits and strengthen the capacity of the Tanzania's government not only manage natural resources, but ensure it is done by considering gender, youth and social inclusion in biodiversity conservation and natural resource management in Tanzania.”

a7299.speaker: Jackson Kiswaga, Chairperson of the parliamentary committee on Water and Environment
a7299.name: Jackson Kiswaga
a7299.title: Chairperson of the parliamentary committee on Water and Environment
a7299.speech: “As policy makers, we are duty bound to remind the government to put up effective plans that will see no one is left behind in the management of the country's natural resources.’’

a7299.speaker: Timotheo Mnzava, chairperson of the parliamentary committee on Natural Resources and Tourism
a7299.name: Timotheo Mnzava
a7299.title: chairperson of the parliamentary committee on Natural Resources and Tourism
a7299.speech: Said that in addressing threats to animal movement and biodiversity, it was high time the government came up with a robust plan for land use. “This plan should make sure that it engages women, youth and special groups,’’ he added.

a7299.speaker: Agness Hokororo, Special Seats MP
a7299.name: Agness Hokororo
a7299.title: Special Seats MP
a7299.speech: According to Special Seats MP, Agness Hokororo, there were many opportunities in wildlife and conservation, however, women were left behind in tapping those opportunities.

a7299.speaker: Rahima Njaidi, MJUMITA Executive Director
a7299.name: Rahima Njaidi
a7299.title: MJUMITA Executive Director
a7299.speech: Emphasised the crucial role of MPs as policymakers in the country. She explained that the awareness training was organised to equip lawmakers with the knowledge and tools needed to advocate for harmonised laws in the wildlife sector.

a7352.speaker: Musa Adamu Ibrahim, Nigerian nurse
a7352.name: Musa Adamu Ibrahim
a7352.title: Nigerian nurse
a7352.speech: “The clinics have been closed and there are no longer any free medicines or mosquito nets. No distribution of preventive measures,” he observed ; the Nigerian nurse laments that these facilities, already threatened by a jihadist insurgency lasting more than 15 years and by criminal armed groups, can no longer operate.

a7352.speaker: Lawrence Barat, former technical adviser to the US President’s Malaria Initiative (PMI)
a7352.name: Lawrence Barat
a7352.title: former technical adviser to the US President’s Malaria Initiative (PMI)
a7352.speech: warns that in sub-Saharan Africa “those who have resources will still be able to obtain medicines… But the poorest, in remote areas (…) will be left behind” ; “It is their children who will die,” he laments.

a7352.speaker: Saschveen Singh, infectious diseases specialist at Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF)
a7352.name: Saschveen Singh
a7352.title: infectious diseases specialist at Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF)
a7352.speech: explains that the strategies put in place by African governments to fight malaria are severely affected; on the Democratic Republic of Congo, where the USAID-backed PMI was the main supplier of medicines and diagnostic tests in public facilities in nine provinces, she estimates that in future “it will no longer have medicines and it will be very difficult for other actors to step in”, adding that her colleagues are “scrambling” to determine where shortages are likely to occur.

a7352.speaker: Save the Children (British NGO)
a7352.name: Save the Children (British NGO)
a7352.speech: reported this month that children walk for hours to reach the nearest treatment centre, and that at least five died on the way in Jonglei State (east) in South Sudan.

a7352.speaker: An elder of the Kakuma refugee camp, Kenya (anonymous)
a7352.name: An elder of the Kakuma refugee camp
a7352.title: Kenya (anonymous)
a7352.speech: told AFP: “In all the clinics round about, you can get paracetamol. But there are no other medicines.”

a7352.speaker: Yvonne Walo, epidemiologist at Kinkole general hospital, Kinshasa
a7352.name: Yvonne Walo
a7352.title: epidemiologist at Kinkole general hospital, Kinshasa
a7352.speech: “We tell ourselves that a catastrophe is coming.”

a7352.speaker: Sania Nishtar, CEO of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance
a7352.name: Sania Nishtar
a7352.title: CEO of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance
a7352.speech: “it is a hole too big to be filled.”

a7352.speaker: Governor of Borno State, Nigeria
a7352.name: Governor of Borno State
a7352.title: Nigeria
a7352.speech: recently warned of the risk of a resurgence of the jihadist group Boko Haram.

a7352.speaker: Kunduli, humanitarian worker recently laid off (Borno State, Nigeria)
a7352.name: Kunduli
a7352.title: humanitarian worker recently laid off (Borno State, Nigeria)
a7352.speech: stresses that the work was already “overwhelming” even with American funding. So without it… “I cannot even imagine it,” she says.

a7376.speaker: United Nations (communiqué)
a7376.name: United Nations (communiqué)
a7376.speech: States in a communiqué released today that the objective is to support 8.2 million people affected by the crisis both inside and outside Ukraine, at a time when the country is about to complete three years at war. ; "Humanitarian organizations in Ukraine intend to help 6 million people in 2025 with food, health care, shelter, financial assistance, emergency education, protection and other vital services." ; "With sufficient funding and access, humanitarian actors can continue to deliver aid across the country, including in communities near the front line." ; The focus will be given to the most vulnerable groups, namely children, the elderly and people with disabilities, "many of whom face isolation and barriers in accessing aid." ; Humanitarian organizations also intend to support 11 host countries in the region, "as they expand protection and include more than 2 million refugees in their national systems in 2025 and 2026", which will allow refugees access to housing, decent work, health care and specialized legal and protection services.

a7376.speaker: United Nations (communiqué)
a7376.name: United Nations (communiqué)
a7376.speech: Noted that last year, despite underfunding and access restrictions, humanitarian partners in Ukraine managed to give food aid to nearly 3 million people and provide water, sanitation and hygiene support to about 5.8 million people, mainly in front-line regions; enabled access to medical and health services for two million people; and that in the refugee-hosting countries partners secured only a third of their financial needs.

a7376.speaker: Ukraine Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (document)
a7376.name: Ukraine Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (document)
a7376.speech: Requires 2.5 billion euros to meet these needs, and highlights the importance of international solidarity to sustain essential humanitarian efforts in 2025.

a7376.speaker: Tom Fletcher, head of the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a7376.name: Tom Fletcher
a7376.title: head of the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a7376.speech: "I am impressed by the determination of the Ukrainian people to move forward in the face of immense hardship." ; "These communities are the front line of the humanitarian response and they need our support and solidarity more than ever." ; "Now, we need the international community to seriously support these plans so that we can show the same power of resilience as the people of Ukraine."

a7376.speaker: Filippo Grandi, United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
a7376.name: Filippo Grandi
a7376.title: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
a7376.speech: Referred to a visit to several countries that have hosted Ukrainian refugees, stressing that the international community cannot now forget "the millions of Ukrainians who were forced to flee their homes and, in the case of many, their country"; said the countries hosting Ukrainian refugees "have done incredible work over the last three years to provide safety and a sense of normality" to those who have to restart their lives in new communities, and that it is necessary to "continue to sustain the hope" that has been provided.

a7384.speaker: Africanews (report)
a7384.name: Africanews (report)
a7384.speech: Writes that at Kyeshero Hospital in Goma the beds are full of patients with traumatic injuries.

a7384.speaker: United Nations
a7384.name: United Nations
a7384.speech: According to the UN, the M23 rebels are backed by about 4,000 troops from neighbouring Rwanda, far more than in 2012, when they captured Goma for the first time and held it for days.

a7401.speaker: Zwelini Mkhize, South African Health Minister
a7401.name: Zwelini Mkhize
a7401.title: South African Health Minister
a7401.speech: Announced 10,107 new cases Saturday night, bringing the country's cumulative total to 503,290, including 8,153 deaths.

a7401.speaker: Johns Hopkins University (tally)
a7401.name: Johns Hopkins University (tally)
a7401.speech: According to its tally, South Africa, with a population of about 58 million, has the fifth-highest number of cases in the world, behind the U.S., Brazil, Russia and India, all countries with significantly higher populations.

a7401.speaker: Experts
a7401.name: Experts
a7401.speech: Say the true toll of the pandemic worldwide is much higher than confirmed cases, because of limited testing and other reasons.

a7401.speaker: Denis Chopera, virologist based in Durban, executive manager of the Sub-Saharan African Network for TB/HIV Research Excellence
a7401.name: Denis Chopera
a7401.title: virologist based in Durban, executive manager of the Sub-Saharan African Network for TB/HIV Research Excellence
a7401.speech: “Half a million is a significant milestone, because it shows we've entered a stage of rapid increases. We may reach 1 million cases very quickly” ; “What we know for sure is that the figures are an underestimate and that this virus will be with us for a long time to come.”

a7401.speaker: Denis Chopera, virologist based in Durban, executive manager of the Sub-Saharan African Network for TB/HIV Research Excellence
a7401.name: Denis Chopera
a7401.title: virologist based in Durban, executive manager of the Sub-Saharan African Network for TB/HIV Research Excellence
a7401.speech: Said South Africa will have multiple peaks across the country, each challenging its different provincial health care systems: “The Western Cape had the first peak and did relatively well. Gauteng is the epicentre now and appears to be coping so far” ; “Other provinces, like the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal, do not have reputations for well-organized health care systems. They may have serious problems.”

a7401.speaker: Health experts
a7401.name: Health experts
a7401.speech: Say the country could reach the peak of its outbreak in late August or early September; according to health experts, Cape Town was the first epicentre and reached its peak last month.

a7401.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, South African President
a7401.name: Cyril Ramaphosa
a7401.title: South African President
a7401.speech: Has warned that now, more than ever, South Africa's persistent problem with widespread graft is endangering people's lives.

a7434.speaker: International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) report (Policy Note 53)
a7434.name: International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) report (Policy Note 53)
a7434.speech: Reveals how a sudden suspension of U.S. foreign assistance has sent Malawi spiraling into its worst humanitarian crisis in decades, with nearly half a million citizens expected to fall into extreme poverty by year’s end and critical health services collapsing nationwide; the cuts total $177 million, or 59% of annual American aid ; the report’s findings expose the staggering human toll: 4,451 healthcare workers laid off, 18 HIV treatment centres shuttered, and life-saving maternal health programs nearly eliminated overnight ; the aid suspension has slashed Malawi’s foreign currency reserves by an amount equivalent to 6.3% of annual imports – enough to purchase 3.5 weeks’ worth of essential goods ; IFPRI economists project Malawi’s GDP will shrink by 127 million this year alone, with cumulative losses reaching 1.3 billion by 2030, and an additional 435,000 Malawians will sink below the poverty line in 2025 ; the health sector, which received 57% of U.S. assistance according to the report, faces particularly brutal cuts, with HIV/AIDS programs losing 36-39% of funding while maternal and child health initiatives were virtually erased with 96-100% reductions ; agricultural programs crucial to food security have been slashed by 59% ; the report warns the double blow of health system collapse and looming food shortages could create a humanitarian catastrophe.

a7434.speaker: Dr. Grace Mwale, a physician in Lilongwe
a7434.name: Dr. Grace Mwale
a7434.title: a physician in Lilongwe
a7434.speech: “These aren’t just numbers in a report – these are mothers who can’t get prenatal care, HIV patients turned away from clinics, and children going hungry” ; “We’re watching years of progress unravel before our eyes.”

a7434.speaker: Jan Duchoslav of IFPRI, report co-author
a7434.name: Jan Duchoslav of IFPRI
a7434.title: report co-author
a7434.speech: “This aid wasn’t charity – it was keeping people alive” ; “The data shows that without urgent intervention, we’ll see needless deaths from preventable causes in the coming months.”

a7434.speaker: Esther Phiri, 32-year-old resident of Ntcheu village
a7434.name: Esther Phiri
a7434.title: 32-year-old resident of Ntcheu village
a7434.speech: “I pray every night that someone will help us” ; “But the numbers in this report show that help is disappearing when we need it most.”
